explanation.summary: Imperforate hymen is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract and results from failure of the hymenal membrane to canalise at the junction of the sinovaginal bulb and urogenital sinus. Because ovarian function and the endometrium are normal, girls develop normally through puberty and present only when menstrual blood accumulates, typically at thirteen to fifteen years with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea. Accumulated blood distends the vagina and later the uterus, producing a palpable pelvic mass that can compress the bladder neck and cause acute urinary retention, or the rectum and cause constipation. The examination that makes the diagnosis is simple inspection of the vulva, which is why the condition is often missed for months when the abdomen alone is examined. Definitive treatment is surgical hymenotomy under general anaesthesia, and outcomes including future fertility are excellent once the obstruction is relieved.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain and no menses is the classic triad.
Vulval inspection shows a tense bulging bluish membrane and makes the diagnosis.
Urinary retention or constipation reflects mass effect from the distended vagina.
Androgen insensitivity also gives primary amenorrhoea but with absent pubic hair and no collection.
Definitive management is surgical hymenotomy, not aspiration.
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent presenting with acute urinary retention and no neurological cause should have the vulva inspected before imaging is ordered, because haematocolpos from an imperforate hymen is the diagnosis that a two minute examination makes and an abdominal examination alone will miss.

options.rationale: Menstrual suppression is a legitimate temporising measure when definitive surgery must be delayed, which is why it is tempting here. It does nothing for an existing collection or for the retention it is causing, so it cannot be the primary step. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Karyotype and androgen testing investigate complete androgen insensitivity, which also presents with primary amenorrhoea and normal breast development. That condition gives absent or sparse pubic hair and a blind ending vagina without an obstructed distended collection. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

Needle aspiration decompresses the collection briefly but leaves the obstruction intact, so it refills, and puncturing a closed space risks converting sterile old blood into a pyocolpos. Formal incision with drainage is the standard. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Imperforate hymen)

Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics, cyclical pain and a bulging bluish membrane is an imperforate hymen with haematocolpos, and urinary retention makes it urgent. Catheterisation relieves the retention while definitive surgical hymenotomy under anaesthesia drains the obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

Outpatient imaging would be sensible for cyclical pain without retention, and ultrasound does confirm the diagnosis. Waiting a month with a bladder residual of 480 mL risks upper tract dilatation and continued retrograde menstruation. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without identifiable pelvic pathology and affects up to three quarters of adolescents, making it a leading cause of school absence in this age group. Pain arises from prostaglandin F2 alpha released by the shedding endometrium, which causes myometrial contraction and ischaemia, and the same prostaglandins explain the accompanying nausea and diarrhoea. It characteristically begins six to twenty four months after menarche, once ovulatory cycles are established, and is confined to the first day or two of bleeding. Features that should prompt reconsideration include onset with the very first period, pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, and failure to respond to adequate medical treatment, all of which raise endometriosis or an obstructive anomaly. Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, combined hormonal contraception is the usual next step, and the two can be used together.
key_points: Onset six to twenty four months after menarche with pain confined to the bleeding days.
Prostaglandin mediated, which is why non-steroidal agents outperform paracetamol.
Dosing should begin before or at the onset of bleeding, not after pain is established.
Combined hormonal contraception is second line or first when contraception is wanted.
Pain outside menstruation or treatment failure should prompt evaluation for endometriosis.
explanation.pearls: Mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily, started one day before the expected period and continued for the first two to three days, is the standard Australian regimen, and taking it pre emptively rather than reactively is what converts a partial response into a complete one.

options.rationale: Laparoscopy investigates endometriosis, which is suggested by pain extending beyond the bleeding days, deep pain with intercourse, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, or failure of medical treatment. None of those features is present and no treatment has yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

Imaging is reserved for atypical features, an abnormal examination or treatment failure, and transvaginal scanning is inappropriate in a young woman who is not sexually active. A normal scan would not change first line management. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

Pain beginning within two years of menarche with regular cycles and no symptoms between periods is primary dysmenorrhoea, driven by endometrial prostaglandin release. Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis is the mechanism specific treatment and works best when started before or at the onset of bleeding rather than once the pain is established. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

Regular rather than as needed dosing is a genuine improvement on what she is doing and is a reasonable adjunct, so this is the closest wrong answer. Paracetamol does not inhibit peripheral prostaglandin synthesis in the endometrium and is consistently less effective than a non-steroidal agent for this indication. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Combined hormonal contraception is effective and is the usual second line, or the first choice when contraception is also wanted. It is not the initial step for an adolescent whose simple analgesia has never been optimised and who has not tried a prostaglandin inhibitor. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Endometrial polyps are focal overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma with a fibrovascular core, and they are a common structural cause of intermenstrual bleeding in women in their thirties and forties. On transvaginal ultrasound they appear as well defined echogenic intracavity lesions, and the single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, sometimes called the pedicle artery sign, is characteristic. The key management principle is that focal lesions need focal sampling: blind endometrial biopsy is designed for diffuse pathology and has poor sensitivity for a discrete polyp, so hysteroscopy is required. Malignancy within a polyp is uncommon in premenopausal women at well under two per cent, but rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size, so histology is always obtained. Saline infusion sonohysterography is an alternative way of delineating the cavity where hysteroscopy access is limited.
key_points: Intermenstrual bleeding with a discrete echogenic intracavity lesion suggests a polyp.
A single feeding vessel on colour Doppler supports the diagnosis.
Blind pipelle sampling has poor sensitivity for focal lesions.
Hysteroscopic resection is diagnostic and therapeutic in the same procedure.
Malignancy risk rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size.
explanation.pearls: Measure the endometrium on days five to ten of the cycle when a scan is being arranged for abnormal bleeding in a premenopausal woman, because a secretory phase endometrium can measure over 14 mm normally and generates unnecessary referrals.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling reliably detects diffuse endometrial pathology such as hyperplasia or carcinoma, but it samples only a fraction of the cavity and frequently misses a focal lesion entirely. A negative result would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.rationale: Timing a scan to days five to ten is the right way to reduce false positives when the endometrium looks thickened and non-specific, since secretory endometrium can mimic pathology. A discrete lesion with its own feeding vessel is already a definite finding. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces menstrual blood loss but has no effect on intermenstrual spotting from a structural lesion, and her blood count is normal so volume is not the problem. This treats the wrong element of her presentation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A well defined echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel is an endometrial polyp, and hysteroscopic resection under direct vision both cures the bleeding and provides tissue. It is the definitive investigation and treatment in one procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.rationale: The intrauterine system is excellent for heavy menstrual bleeding once the cavity is known to be normal, and it does thin the endometrium. Placing it over an undiagnosed focal lesion leaves the pathology in place and commonly causes further unscheduled bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, producing a diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heavy painful periods and a characteristic dragging pelvic heaviness. Ultrasound features include a globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, linear striations and a thickened or irregular junctional zone, with a junctional zone of 12 mm or more being widely used as a threshold. It is increasingly recognised as a contributor to subfertility and to miscarriage and preterm birth, probably through disrupted junctional zone peristalsis and impaired implantation. The central management tension is that the effective treatments, including the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonists, continuous progestogens and embolisation, are all incompatible with conceiving. For the woman trying to conceive, treatment is therefore limited to fertility sparing symptom control with iron replacement, tranexamic acid and non-steroidal analgesia, alongside prompt referral for assisted reproduction where indicated.
key_points: Globular tender uterus with junctional zone thickening above 12 mm suggests adenomyosis.
Endometriosis is distinguished by uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus.
Most effective treatments are contraceptive and therefore unavailable when conception is the goal.
Correct iron deficiency and use tranexamic acid for bleeding while fertility is being pursued.
Adenomyosis is associated with subfertility, miscarriage and preterm birth.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g three to four times daily for the first three to four days of bleeding reduces menstrual blood loss by roughly 40 per cent without affecting ovulation or conception, which makes it the workhorse for heavy bleeding in a woman actively trying to become pregnant.

options.rationale: The intrauterine system is the most effective medical treatment for adenomyosis and would be the right answer for a woman not seeking pregnancy. It is a contraceptive, so recommending it to a woman actively trying to conceive defeats her primary goal. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue and is sometimes used before surgery, but it induces a hypo oestrogenic anovulatory state and so prevents conception throughout treatment. It also carries bone density consequences over that timeframe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Junctional zone thickening above 12 mm with a globular tender uterus and myometrial cysts is adenomyosis, and every effective suppressive treatment for it prevents conception. In a woman with an eleven month history of trying, the plan is symptom control that preserves fertility plus timely referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Laparoscopy targets peritoneal endometriosis, which produces uterosacral nodularity, a fixed retroverted uterus and deep pain with intercourse rather than a symmetrically enlarged boggy uterus. Adenomyosis lies within the myometrium and is not diagnosed or treated by looking at the peritoneum. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

Embolisation does improve adenomyosis symptoms but risks ovarian and endometrial injury and is generally avoided in women with a current pregnancy intention. It is offered mainly to women who have completed their families. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Nipple vasospasm is a Raynaud phenomenon of the nipple in which arteriolar constriction follows the temperature drop as the nipple leaves the warm mouth, and it is a frequently missed cause of severe persistent nipple pain in breastfeeding women. The history that identifies it is pain that starts after rather than during the feed, is described as burning or shooting, and is reliably provoked by cold, together with an observable blanching of the nipple tip. The classic triphasic white to blue to red colour change is not always complete, and blanching alone in the right clinical context is enough. It is very commonly misdiagnosed as candidal infection, and many women arrive having already failed courses of antifungal treatment for both themselves and the infant. Underlying poor attachment and nipple trauma can trigger vasospasm, so attachment must still be assessed, but once optimised the treatment is avoidance of cold, immediate warmth after feeds, and nifedipine where conservative measures fail.
key_points: Pain starting after the feed ends and provoked by cold distinguishes vasospasm.
Blanching of the nipple tip, with or without the full triphasic change, is the sign.
It is routinely misdiagnosed and treated as candidal infection without benefit.
Optimise attachment first, since nipple trauma can trigger the vasospasm.
Nifedipine is compatible with breastfeeding and works within days when it is going to work.
explanation.pearls: Nifedipine 20 mg of the modified release preparation once daily is the usual starting dose for nipple vasospasm, with response expected within about 72 hours, and only trivial amounts pass into breast milk so the infant needs no monitoring.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.rationale: Poor attachment and restrictive tongue tie are the commonest causes of nipple pain overall and would be the first thing to address, which is why this remains tempting. Attachment has already been assessed as satisfactory and the infant is gaining well, and neither explains cold provoked colour change. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.rationale: Extended antifungal therapy for mother and infant is the standard approach to candidal nipple infection, which gives a persistent burning pain that is present during as well as after feeds and is usually accompanied by shiny or flaky areolar skin or infant oral thrush. She has already failed adequate antifungal treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A triphasic colour change with pain beginning after the feed and provoked by cold is vasospasm of the nipple, a Raynaud phenomenon, not infection. Conservative warming plus a calcium channel blocker is the established treatment and breastfeeding can continue throughout. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.rationale: Resting the nipples helps a mechanical or traumatic injury heal, but vasospasm is triggered by the temperature drop when the nipple is exposed to air, which expressing does not avoid. It also risks undermining supply at six weeks. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal therapy treats mastitis or an infected nipple fissure, which produces a red tender wedge of breast with systemic symptoms or a visibly broken nipple surface. Her breasts are soft and her nipple skin is intact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder is the current diagnostic term that unified what were previously called vaginismus and dyspareunia, and it covers difficulty with penetration, vulvovaginal pain on attempted penetration, fear of that pain, and involuntary pelvic floor tightening. Lifelong forms present exactly as this woman does, with tampons, examinations and intercourse all impossible from the outset and a structurally normal genital tract. A pain and fear cycle sustains the condition: anticipation increases pelvic floor tone, the increased tone makes penetration painful, and the pain reinforces the anticipation. Assessment must still exclude organic causes including lichen sclerosus, vulval dermatoses, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism, which is why unhurried inspection matters even when internal examination is declined. Treatment combines pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded self directed dilator work and psychosexual therapy, ideally with the partner involved, and success rates with this combination are high.
key_points: Involuntary pelvic floor contraction with a structurally normal vulva defines the disorder.
Lifelong forms prevent tampon use and clinical examination as well as intercourse.
Exclude lichen sclerosus, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism by inspection.
Pelvic floor physiotherapy plus psychosexual therapy is first line and highly effective.
Never force an internal examination; it reinforces the fear that maintains the condition.
explanation.pearls: Offering the woman control of the pace and of the instrument, including letting her place her own hand over yours or insert a dilator herself, changes outcomes measurably, because loss of control during examination is one of the strongest perpetuating factors in this disorder.

options.rationale: Lifelong inability to tolerate penetration with involuntary pelvic floor contraction and a normal vulva is genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder, in which the muscle response and the anticipatory fear maintain each other. Combined pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

Surgery addresses an anatomical obstruction such as a microperforate hymen or a transverse vaginal septum. The hymenal ring is patent on inspection here, and operating on a normal introitus reinforces the belief that something is physically wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

Botulinum toxin is studied as a third line option for refractory cases and is not first line, since it does not address the cognitive and behavioural components. Offering it before conservative therapy exposes her to an invasive procedure with modest evidence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vaginismus)

Vaginal oestrogen treats the thin pale friable epithelium of genitourinary syndrome of menopause or of prolonged lactational hypo oestrogenism. A well oestrogenised vulva in a 26-year-old with normal cycles will not respond to it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Topical anaesthetic is a reasonable adjunct that some women use alongside desensitisation work, so it is not a wrong treatment in itself. Used alone it numbs the vestibular pain without addressing the involuntary muscle response that physically prevents penetration. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, and childcare and primary school staff are the classic occupational exposure group. Infected children are contagious in the week before the rash appears and are no longer infectious once it is visible, so exposure has usually already occurred by the time an outbreak is recognised. Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the highest fetal risk because the virus targets erythroid precursors, and the fetus of that gestation has rapid red cell turnover and limited marrow reserve, producing anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Vertical transmission occurs in roughly a third of maternal infections and hydrops develops in a few per cent, typically two to six weeks after maternal infection. Management after a confirmed maternal infection is serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity measurement, and intrauterine transfusion where anaemia is detected, which achieves good survival.
key_points: Children are infectious before the rash appears, not after it.
About 60 per cent of women of childbearing age are already immune, so test serology first.
Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the greatest risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops.
Confirmed infection is followed with serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity.
Intrauterine transfusion treats detected fetal anaemia with good survival.
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median for gestational age is the threshold that triggers referral for fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion, and it detects significant anaemia non invasively with sensitivity above 90 per cent.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

options.rationale: Serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is exactly the right surveillance once maternal infection is confirmed, and it is what detects fetal anaemia. Starting it before serology commits an already immune woman to fourteen weeks of unnecessary scans. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

The risk is real between about 9 and 20 weeks, when the fetal liver is the main site of erythropoiesis and red cell lifespan is short, which is precisely the window she is in. Vertical transmission occurs in around a third of maternal infections. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

Amniotic fluid testing confirms fetal infection but is invasive and is reserved for cases where fetal anaemia or hydrops is already suspected on ultrasound. It is not a screening test after an exposure. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

Post exposure immunoglobulin is effective for varicella and for measles but there is no established prophylaxis against parvovirus B19 in pregnancy. Offering it implies a protection that does not exist. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Around 60 per cent of Australian women of childbearing age are already immune to parvovirus B19, so serology first establishes whether she is at any risk at all before committing to surveillance. Immunoglobulin G positive with immunoglobulin M negative means past infection and needs nothing further. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Erosive lichen planus is an immune mediated mucocutaneous disease that affects the vulva, vagina and mouth and is the most disabling of the vulval dermatoses. The vulvovaginal gingival syndrome describes the combination of erosive vulval and vaginal disease with desquamative gingivitis, and asking about the mouth often unlocks a diagnosis that has been missed for years. The physical signs that separate it from lichen sclerosus are its involvement of the vestibule and vagina, the glazed erosive surface, the lacy white reticular Wickham striae at the border, and the raised vaginal pH from the associated vaginitis. Untreated disease causes progressive scarring with labial resorption, introital narrowing and vaginal stenosis, and it carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk of the order of one to three per cent. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol, with calcineurin inhibitors, vaginal preparations or systemic immunosuppression added for resistant disease, and long term surveillance is required.
key_points: Erosive lichen planus involves the vagina and vestibule; lichen sclerosus spares the vagina.
A lacy white reticular border and oral striae are the discriminating findings.
Repeated failed antifungal courses should prompt reassessment of the diagnosis.
Biopsy from the edge of the lesion confirms the diagnosis and establishes a baseline.
Scarring causes labial fusion and vaginal stenosis, and malignant transformation can occur.
explanation.pearls: A vaginal pH above 4.5 in a woman with vulval symptoms points to vaginal involvement, which occurs in erosive lichen planus and desquamative inflammatory vaginitis but essentially never in lichen sclerosus, so a strip of indicator paper separates the two dermatoses at the bedside.

options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is used for recurrent candidiasis, which she does not have on repeated swabs and which does not fuse the labia or narrow the introitus. Six failed courses should already have prompted a change of diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Surgery has a place once the inflammatory disease is controlled, because operating on actively inflamed tissue leads to rapid re adhesion through the same process that caused the fusion. Medical control comes first, with dilators used as an adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

The treatment is right but the diagnosis is not: lichen sclerosus gives white parchment like atrophic skin over the labia, perineum and perianal area in a figure of eight, with ecchymosis and fissuring, and it spares the vagina. Erosive lichen planus involves the vestibule and vagina and produces the reticular border seen here. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which produces a uniformly pale thin friable epithelium rather than a sharply demarcated erosion with a reticular border. She has already failed a course of it, which argues against that diagnosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Glazed erosive vestibular erythema with a lacy reticular border and matching buccal striae is erosive lichen planus, which is confirmed histologically and treated with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid. Biopsy also establishes a baseline because the condition carries a malignant potential. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary caused by severe postpartum haemorrhage and hypotension, made possible by the physiological enlargement of the lactotroph rich gland during pregnancy within a fixed bony fossa. Presentation is often delayed by months or years because the deficiencies accumulate gradually, and the two earliest and most specific clues are failure to lactate and failure of menses to return. Anterior pituitary hormones are typically lost in a characteristic order, with growth hormone and gonadotrophins going first, then adrenocorticotrophic hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone, while the posterior pituitary is usually spared. Hyponatraemia is common and reflects cortisol deficiency impairing free water excretion rather than true salt loss. The diagnosis matters because unrecognised secondary adrenal insufficiency can present as adrenal crisis during an intercurrent illness, and glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating one.
key_points: Failure of lactation plus failure of menses to return after major haemorrhage is the hallmark.
Presentation is frequently delayed by months to years after the index birth.
In secondary hypothyroidism the thyroid stimulating hormone is normal or low, not raised.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium suggests a secondary rather than primary adrenal cause.
Replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Starting thyroxine before hydrocortisone in any form of hypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis within days, because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance, so the order of replacement is not a matter of preference.

options.rationale: Failure of lactation and amenorrhoea after a haemorrhage needing massive transfusion, with postural hypotension and hyponatraemia, is Sheehan syndrome from pituitary infarction. A combined anterior pituitary panel with a morning cortisol identifies which axes have failed and how urgently replacement is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Screening for postnatal depression is appropriate in any tired new mother and the overlap of symptoms is real. It does not account for absent lactation, postural hypotension, loss of body hair or hyponatraemia, all of which are endocrine findings. (Source: COPE: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

This workup is directed at primary adrenal insufficiency, which is distinguished by hyperpigmentation, hyperkalaemia and a raised adrenocorticotrophic hormone because the adrenal itself has failed. Normal potassium and no pigmentation point to a secondary cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

This combination investigates secondary amenorrhoea from a prolactinoma or premature ovarian insufficiency and would be reasonable if amenorrhoea were the only problem. It misses the adrenal and thyroid axes, and it is the cortisol deficiency here that is potentially fatal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

This panel targets postpartum thyroiditis and iron deficiency, which are far commoner causes of postnatal fatigue and are worth having. In pituitary failure the thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal or low despite a low free thyroxine, so measuring it alone gives false reassurance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Missing intrauterine device threads is a common presentation and the assessment follows a fixed sequence: exclude pregnancy, look in the canal, image the uterus, and if the cavity is empty, image the abdomen. Where ultrasound shows no device in the uterus, the two possibilities are expulsion, which occurs in about one in twenty users and is commonest in the first year, and uterine perforation, which occurs in around one to two per thousand insertions. Perforation risk is increased roughly six fold by insertion while breastfeeding and is also higher when insertion occurs within six months of delivery, because the uterus is soft and involuting. Critically, perforation is silent in a substantial minority, so a painless history and normal subsequent periods do not exclude it, and a plain abdominal radiograph is mandatory before a replacement device is inserted. A confirmed intra abdominal device is retrieved laparoscopically because copper in particular incites an inflammatory reaction with adhesions and occasional bowel or bladder erosion.
key_points: Sequence is pregnancy test, canal inspection, pelvic ultrasound, then abdominal radiograph.
An empty cavity means either expulsion or perforation, which cannot be told apart clinically.
Breastfeeding at insertion and insertion within six months of delivery both raise perforation risk.
Up to a third of perforations are asymptomatic, so a painless history excludes nothing.
Never reinsert a device until the abdominal film has excluded a migrated one.
explanation.pearls: Both copper and levonorgestrel devices are radio opaque, so a single plain abdominal film from diaphragm to pelvic floor answers the question in minutes; the common error is limiting the film to the pelvis, which misses devices that have migrated into the omentum or upper abdomen.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: Intrauterine contraception

options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is used when the device is known to be intrauterine but embedded or with retracted threads. A cavity already shown to be empty on ultrasound will simply be confirmed as empty, and the device is not inside it. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is the correct retrieval procedure once an intra abdominal device is confirmed, and it is what she will need if the film is positive. Operating before localising the device commits her to an anaesthetic that is unnecessary if it was simply expelled. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.rationale: Transabdominal scanning widens the field beyond the transvaginal view and is a reasonable adjunct, but a device that has migrated into the upper abdomen or omentum lies outside the pelvic field and is easily missed on ultrasound of any window. Radiography covers the whole cavity in one image. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.rationale: Expulsion is the commoner of the two outcomes and she has had regular periods since, which makes this genuinely tempting. Reinserting without excluding an intra abdominal device leaves a perforated device in the peritoneal cavity where it can cause adhesions or bowel injury. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.rationale: An empty uterus on ultrasound has two explanations, expulsion and perforation, and they cannot be distinguished clinically because up to a third of perforations are painless. A plain film of the whole abdomen and pelvis is the test that finds or excludes a migrated radio opaque device. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture is one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, and after the age of 50 it establishes a clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis regardless of the bone density result, which matters because around half of all fragility fractures occur in people whose T score falls in the osteopenic range rather than below minus 2.5. The single strongest predictor of a future fracture is a past fracture, and the risk is highest in the first two years afterwards, a window often described as the imminent fracture risk period. This is the rationale for fracture liaison services and for starting treatment promptly rather than waiting for a densitometry threshold to be crossed. Secondary causes should be screened for before treatment, covering calcium, vitamin D, renal and thyroid function, and a paraprotein, with coeliac serology and testosterone considered in selected patients. Oral bisphosphonates are first line in Australia, with adherence being the main practical limitation, and denosumab or an anabolic agent reserved for intolerance, contraindication or very high risk.
key_points: A fall from standing height causing fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically
Around half of fragility fractures occur in people with osteopenic rather than osteoporotic scores
Risk of a further fracture is highest in the first two years
Screen for secondary causes before starting treatment
Denosumab requires strict continuity because cessation causes rapid bone loss
explanation.pearls: Never stop denosumab without transitioning to a bisphosphonate, because the rebound increase in bone turnover after a missed six monthly dose can cause multiple vertebral fractures within a year, a risk that does not follow cessation of bisphosphonate therapy.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.rationale: Lifestyle advice with repeat densitometry would suit a woman with this T score and no fracture. A fracture from a fall at standing height after the age of 50 establishes the diagnosis independently of the densitometry and identifies her as being at high risk of a further fracture in the next two years. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.rationale: Denosumab is an effective antiresorptive and is used where bisphosphonates are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. It requires strict continuity, because stopping it without transitioning to another agent produces rapid bone loss and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, so it is not the first choice in an otherwise straightforward case. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and reduces fracture, and it is a reasonable choice for a woman in her early fifties who also has vasomotor symptoms. At 62 and eleven years past her final period it is not started for bone protection alone, because the balance of cardiovascular and thrombotic risk shifts with time since menopause. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

A minimal trauma fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically whatever the T score shows, and it is also the criterion under which antiresorptive therapy is subsidised in Australia. Oral bisphosphonate is the first line agent, with adequate calcium intake and vitamin D as supportive measures rather than as treatment in themselves. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D support the action of antiresorptive therapy but do not meaningfully reduce fracture risk on their own in someone who has already sustained a minimal trauma fracture. Her vitamin D is already within normal limits. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium with surrounding smooth muscle hypertrophy, and it classically presents in the fourth and fifth decades with the combination of heavy menstrual bleeding and progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea that begins before the bleeding starts. Examination typically finds a diffusely bulky, globular and tender uterus, in contrast to the irregular firm non-tender uterus of fibroid disease, and this distinction carries through to imaging. The ultrasound features are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, subendometrial echogenic lines and buds, and an indistinct or thickened junctional zone, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for cases where ultrasound is equivocal or surgical planning is needed. Because the process is diffuse rather than focal, treatments directed at discrete lesions such as myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation are less reliable than they are for fibroids. The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line, combined hormonal or continuous progestogen therapy is second line, and hysterectomy remains definitive for women who have completed their family and in whom medical management has failed.
key_points: Heavy bleeding with dysmenorrhoea starting before the bleeding is the characteristic pattern
A globular tender bulky uterus contrasts with the irregular firm uterus of fibroids
Ultrasound shows myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone without a discrete lesion
The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line treatment
Check ferritin, because iron deficiency is usually present before anaemia appears
explanation.pearls: Check ferritin as well as haemoglobin in every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, because iron stores are exhausted long before the haemoglobin falls and treating the deficiency resolves the fatigue that patients often attribute to the bleeding itself.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Induced hypo-oestrogenism does shrink the uterus and reduce bleeding, but it is used for short term control before surgery rather than as ongoing treatment because of bone loss and vasomotor effects. Symptoms return once it is stopped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive and is appropriate where medical treatment fails or is declined, but proceeding to major surgery before any hormonal treatment has been tried is a substantial escalation. Most women in this situation obtain adequate control medically. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Continuous combined oral contraception is a reasonable second line option that reduces bleeding and dysmenorrhoea, and it suits women who prefer an oral method. It is less effective than the intrauterine route for heavy bleeding and carries a thrombotic risk that the local method does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces bleeding volume by around a third and is useful as an adjunct or for women wanting non hormonal treatment. It does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea, which is half of her problem here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Local progestogen delivery thins the endometrium and acts directly on the myometrium, reducing both bleeding volume and the associated pain, and it is the recommended first line treatment for this condition. It also treats the iron deficiency driver by reducing ongoing loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome of urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia and with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology. Separating it from stress incontinence matters because the treatments differ entirely, and the history plus a cough stress test usually achieves this, with mixed patterns being common and managed by treating the more bothersome component first. The initial assessment excludes the conditions that mimic it, principally urinary infection, diabetes, a pelvic mass, incomplete emptying and haematuria requiring investigation, and a three day bladder diary is the single most informative tool because it quantifies volumes, frequency and fluid intake. First line management is behavioural: bladder training to extend voiding intervals, reduction of caffeine and alcohol, sensible fluid intake and supervised pelvic floor muscle training, which together produce meaningful improvement in a majority. Pharmacotherapy follows, with selective antimuscarinics or a beta 3 agonist preferred over oxybutynin because of anticholinergic burden, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Urgency without leakage on coughing distinguishes this from stress incontinence
Exclude infection, diabetes, incomplete emptying and haematuria first
A three day bladder diary is the most informative single assessment tool
Behavioural treatment is first line and matches drug therapy for effectiveness
Avoid oxybutynin in older women because of anticholinergic cognitive burden
explanation.pearls: Cumulative anticholinergic exposure, including from oxybutynin prescribed for bladder symptoms, is associated with an increased risk of dementia in older women, which is why a beta 3 agonist or a more selective antimuscarinic is preferred once behavioural treatment has been tried.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Behavioural treatment is first line for urinary urgency and produces improvement rates comparable to drug therapy without adverse effects. Bladder training progressively extends the interval between voids, and her six cups of coffee daily represent a substantial and readily modifiable bladder irritant. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy is second line after behavioural measures have been tried, and oxybutynin specifically has the highest anticholinergic burden of the available agents, with cumulative exposure linked to cognitive decline in older women. If a drug were indicated, a more selective agent would be preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a sound pharmacological choice for this condition, so the drug itself is not the error. It still belongs after a trial of behavioural treatment rather than instead of one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Urodynamic testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, mixed or complicated symptoms, or failure of initial treatment, and it is invasive and uncomfortable. Her history, bladder diary, negative cough stress test and normal residual volume already identify the pattern. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A sling supports the urethra and treats leakage provoked by a rise in abdominal pressure, which is the opposite mechanism to hers and which her negative cough stress test excludes. Placing a sling for urgency can worsen symptoms and cause voiding dysfunction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts into the vestibule, where obstruction produces a cyst that may be asymptomatic and require no treatment, while secondary infection produces an abscess with rapidly increasing pain over a few days. The organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a single sexually transmitted pathogen, although screening for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is appropriate because both occur. Definitive treatment is drainage combined with a technique that keeps the tract open, since the underlying problem is duct obstruction rather than infection alone, and a Word catheter left in place for two to four weeks allows epithelialisation of a new drainage tract with recurrence rates well below those of simple incision. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, immunosuppression or a confirmed sexually transmitted pathogen. In a woman over 40, particularly with a firm or irregular mass, biopsy should be considered because carcinoma of the gland, although rare, presents in this way.
key_points: The underlying problem is duct obstruction, so drainage must keep a tract open
A Word catheter left for two to four weeks allows a new tract to epithelialise
Simple incision alone recurs in around a third of cases
Antibiotics are reserved for cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression
Consider biopsy in a woman over 40 with a firm or irregular vulval mass
explanation.pearls: A Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 that is firm, irregular or fails to resolve after drainage should be biopsied rather than simply re-drained, because adenocarcinoma of the gland presents exactly as a recurrent cyst and is easily mistaken for one.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate an established collection adequately and leave the pain untreated. They are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression, none of which applies here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Drainage relieves the pain immediately, and leaving a small balloon catheter in the cavity for several weeks allows an epithelialised tract to form so that the gland can continue to drain. This reduces recurrence substantially compared with drainage alone and can be done under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Simple drainage relieves the acute pain effectively, which is why it remains common practice, but the incision seals within days and the gland duct remains obstructed, giving recurrence rates of around a third. The catheter is what converts a temporary measure into a durable one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Marsupialisation creates a permanent drainage opening and is an effective alternative, generally reserved for recurrent disease or for failure of catheter treatment. It requires theatre and anaesthesia for a problem that can be managed today under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Aspiration alone gives short lived relief because the cavity refills rapidly once the needle is withdrawn, and recurrence rates approach 100 per cent. It does not create a tract for ongoing drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Counselling before permanent contraception has to establish that the person understands the method is intended to be irreversible, that reversal surgery is not funded, is often unsuccessful and is not a realistic fallback, and that in vitro fertilisation is the usual route to a later pregnancy. The failure rate of tubal occlusion is roughly one in 200 over a lifetime, which is higher than many people expect and higher than that of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system or an etonogestrel implant, and a pregnancy after tubal occlusion carries a substantially increased chance of being ectopic, which is why it must be excluded promptly if a period is missed. Vasectomy should be discussed in every consultation of this kind because it is performed under local anaesthetic, has fewer complications, lower cost and a lower failure rate. Regret is more likely with younger age, lower parity, recent childbirth or relationship change, and identifying these prompts a fuller discussion rather than a refusal. Timing relative to a caesarean birth or the postpartum period is also addressed, since decisions made around delivery carry a higher rate of subsequent regret.
key_points: Valid consent requires correcting specific misunderstandings about reversibility
Lifetime failure is roughly one in 200 and a later pregnancy is often ectopic
Long-acting reversible methods match or better this failure rate and are reversible
Vasectomy is lower risk, lower cost and more effective and must be discussed
Younger age and recent childbirth predict regret and prompt fuller discussion, not refusal
explanation.pearls: Any woman who misses a period after tubal occlusion needs a pregnancy test and, if positive, urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy, because a substantial proportion of the small number of post procedure pregnancies implant outside the uterus.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A long-acting reversible method has a failure rate at least as low as tubal occlusion and should certainly be presented as an option, so the method itself is entirely reasonable. Substituting it for the procedure she has requested without discussion overrides her expressed preference. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Referring a patient who believes the procedure is reversible and requires no anaesthetic sends her toward an operation she has not actually consented to. The misunderstanding must be corrected first, whether by you or explicitly at the specialist visit. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: She holds two specific factual misunderstandings, about reversibility and about the anaesthetic required, and consent cannot be valid while they stand. Counselling covers permanence, the operative and anaesthetic risks, the failure rate with its ectopic implications, and comparison with long-acting reversible methods and vasectomy, after which referral proceeds if she still wishes it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Vasectomy is a lower risk, lower cost and more effective procedure and belongs in the discussion. Redirecting the request to a partner who is not your patient and has not been assessed bypasses her own decision making. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Age and parity are associated with later regret at a population level but are not grounds for refusing a competent adult's request. Refusal without counselling substitutes the clinician's judgement for the patient's. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on the woman's quality of life rather than by a measured volume, and the assessment establishes whether there is structural pathology, whether the endometrium needs sampling and whether a bleeding disorder is present. Endometrial sampling is indicated with intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, in women over 45, or where medical treatment has failed, and a coagulation screen is warranted where heavy bleeding has been present since menarche. Treatment escalates from tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, through the levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system as the most effective medical option, to surgical management. Endometrial ablation destroys the endometrium and is suited to women who have completed their family, have a normal or near normal cavity and have benign histology, achieving amenorrhoea or acceptable light bleeding in most. Two caveats matter: reliable contraception must continue because a pregnancy after ablation carries high risks of abnormal placentation and miscarriage, and ablation is avoided where the cavity is distorted or where there is atypical hyperplasia, since it obscures later endometrial assessment.
key_points: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by impact on quality of life, not measured volume
Sample the endometrium in women over 45 or where medical treatment has failed
Ablation suits a normal cavity with benign histology and a completed family
Contraception must continue after ablation because pregnancy carries high risk
Avoid ablation where the cavity is distorted or atypical hyperplasia is present
explanation.pearls: Ablation is not a contraceptive, and a pregnancy in an ablated uterus carries a high rate of miscarriage and abnormal placentation, so confirm a reliable method is in place beforehand rather than assuming the resulting amenorrhoea protects against conception.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This produces amenorrhoea but causes bone loss and vasomotor symptoms and is used for short term control or to thin the endometrium before surgery. Bleeding returns when it stops, so it does not resolve her problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Hysterectomy is definitive and remains appropriate where ablation fails, is unsuitable or is declined after discussion. As the immediate next step it commits her to major surgery when a day case alternative with a high success rate has not been tried. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This method is the most effective medical option and its irregular bleeding usually settles within six months, so a longer first trial would have been reasonable. She persisted for six months and found the result unacceptable, so repeating an identical intervention is unlikely to give a different outcome. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

With a normal cavity, benign histology, a completed family and secure contraception already in place, ablation is the appropriate next step after medical treatment has failed. It is a day case procedure with a much shorter recovery than hysterectomy and achieves satisfactory bleeding control in the large majority. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Embolisation works by infarcting fibroids and is effective where they are the cause of the bleeding. Her ultrasound shows no fibroids, so there is no target lesion for the procedure to treat. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Tubo-ovarian abscess is the most serious complication of pelvic inflammatory disease and should be suspected whenever a woman fails to improve on appropriate outpatient therapy or presents with systemic features and an adnexal mass. The infection is polymicrobial, typically involving anaerobes alongside any initiating sexually transmitted pathogen, which is why regimens must cover anaerobic organisms even when chlamydia or gonorrhoea is identified. Admission criteria for pelvic inflammatory disease include failure of oral therapy, inability to tolerate oral intake, pregnancy, systemic sepsis, a suspected abscess and diagnostic uncertainty where surgical pathology such as appendicitis or ectopic pregnancy remains possible. The majority of abscesses under about 7 to 9 cm resolve with parenteral antibiotics alone, with image guided drainage added for larger collections or for slow response, and surgery reserved for rupture, instability or failure of medical treatment after 48 to 72 hours. Longer term consequences include infertility, chronic pelvic pain and a markedly increased risk of ectopic pregnancy, and partner notification and treatment are an essential part of care.
key_points: Suspect an abscess when outpatient therapy fails or an adnexal mass is present
Infection is polymicrobial and must cover anaerobes regardless of the initiating organism
Failure of oral therapy, vomiting, sepsis or a suspected abscess all mandate admission
Most collections under about 7 to 9 cm resolve on parenteral antibiotics alone
Operate for rupture, instability or failure to respond over 48 to 72 hours
explanation.pearls: A tubo-ovarian abscess is polymicrobial regardless of whether chlamydia or gonorrhoea is found, so anaerobic cover with metronidazole must be continued even after a positive nucleic acid test tempts you to narrow the spectrum.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This regimen is appropriate for uncomplicated outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease in a woman who is systemically well and tolerating oral intake. She meets neither condition, and discharging a septic vomiting patient with a 6 cm collection is unsafe. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

The regimen has already failed over four days and she now has a tachycardia, a temperature of 38.7 degrees and a raised lactate. Continuing an ineffective oral course in a septic patient who is vomiting risks rupture of the collection and peritonitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Immediate surgery is indicated for a ruptured collection, haemodynamic instability that does not respond to resuscitation, or failure of parenteral antibiotics over 48 to 72 hours. Operating before antibiotics have been given removes an ovary and tube that would probably have been preserved. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Image guided drainage is a valuable fertility sparing adjunct for larger collections and is increasingly used. As sole treatment it leaves the underlying polymicrobial infection untreated, and it is combined with parenteral antibiotics rather than substituted for them. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Failure of outpatient oral therapy, systemic sepsis and a complex adnexal collection are each independent indications for admission and parenteral treatment. Most collections of this size respond to intravenous antibiotics, with drainage or surgery reserved for those that do not, so surgical review runs alongside medical treatment rather than replacing it. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable infective, inflammatory, neoplastic or neurological cause, and it is subclassified by whether the pain is localised or generalised and whether it is provoked, spontaneous or mixed. The commonest form is localised provoked pain at the vestibule, in which light touch at the five and seven o'clock positions with a cotton bud reproduces the pain against a background of entirely normal looking skin, and this test is the key examination manoeuvre. Women typically present after a long period of empirical antifungal treatment, and repeated failure of that treatment is itself diagnostically informative. The mechanism involves peripheral sensitisation with increased vestibular nerve fibre density, central sensitisation, and secondary overactivity of the pelvic floor muscles, which explains why physiotherapy is effective and why treatment mirrors that of other persistent pain conditions. Management is multimodal, combining education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, psychological and sexual therapy, topical local anaesthetic before intercourse, and neuromodulating agents such as amitriptyline for more severe or generalised pain, with vestibulectomy reserved for refractory localised disease.
key_points: The cotton bud test reproduces pain at the vestibule against normal looking skin
Repeated failure of empirical antifungal treatment is itself diagnostically useful
Visible whitening, fissuring or architectural loss indicates a dermatosis instead
Pelvic floor overactivity is secondary and is why physiotherapy is first line
Reserve vestibulectomy for localised disease refractory to conservative treatment
explanation.pearls: Map the pain with a moistened cotton bud around the vestibule before any speculum is introduced, because a woman who cannot tolerate light touch at five and seven o'clock will not tolerate a speculum, and attempting one destroys the therapeutic relationship at the first visit.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Pain reproduced by light touch at the vestibule with an entirely normal appearance, together with raised pelvic floor muscle tone, indicates a localised provoked pain condition rather than infection or a dermatosis. Pelvic floor physiotherapy targeting the muscle overactivity, combined with explanation of the mechanism, is first line and the education itself reduces distress in a condition most women have been told is imaginary. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is appropriate for recurrent candidiasis confirmed on testing, which her negative swab and nucleic acid test exclude. Four previous empirical courses have already failed, which is itself evidence against the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Topical corticosteroid is the treatment for lichen sclerosus or lichen planus, both of which produce visible change: whitening, fissuring, scarring and loss of the labia minora or clitoral hood. Her vulval architecture is entirely normal, and prolonged potent steroid to normal vestibular skin risks atrophy. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Vestibulectomy has reasonable success rates in carefully selected women with localised provoked pain, so it is a real treatment for this condition rather than an implausible option. It is reserved for those who have failed conservative measures over an extended period, because it is irreversible and many women improve without it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats pain arising from an atrophic epithelium, which occurs after menopause, during lactation or on some hormonal contraceptives. She is 29 with normal appearing well oestrogenised tissue. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by first establishing whether secondary sexual characteristics have developed, because their presence demonstrates a functioning hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis and redirects the assessment from endocrine causes toward anatomical ones. Normal breast and pubic hair development with cyclical pain and no menstrual flow indicates obstruction of the outflow tract, of which an imperforate hymen is the commonest and most distal example, affecting roughly one in 1000 to 2000 girls. Retained menstrual blood distends the vagina and then the uterus, producing a progressively enlarging pelvic mass that can compress the bladder neck and cause urinary retention, or compress the rectum and cause constipation, and these are frequently what brings the patient in rather than the amenorrhoea itself. The differential includes a transverse vaginal septum, which sits higher and has vaginal tissue below it rather than a thin bulging membrane, and Mullerian agenesis, in which there is no uterus, no retained blood and therefore no cyclical pain. Treatment is surgical incision of the membrane, and outcomes for fertility are generally good, with a recognised risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation during the period of obstruction.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics redirect primary amenorrhoea toward an anatomical cause
Cyclical pain with a pelvic mass indicates retained menstrual blood
Urinary retention or constipation from mass effect is often the presenting complaint
A transverse septum sits higher with vaginal tissue below it rather than a bulging membrane
Mullerian agenesis produces no cyclical pain because there is no functioning uterus
explanation.pearls: Inspect the external genitalia in any adolescent with primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pain before ordering a single blood test, because a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus makes the diagnosis in seconds and no hormonal profile will reveal it.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Endocrine and chromosomal investigation is the correct pathway for primary amenorrhoea with absent or incomplete secondary sexual characteristics, which points to gonadal failure or a central cause. Her breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 4, so the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis is demonstrably working and the problem is mechanical. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Normal pubertal development with cyclical pain, primary amenorrhoea, a pelvic mass of retained menstrual blood and a visible bulging membrane establishes an obstructed outflow tract, and incision under anaesthesia relieves the obstruction and the urinary retention. It is performed in theatre with adequate analgesia and sterility rather than at the bedside. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex obstructive anomalies such as a transverse vaginal septum or an obstructed hemivagina, where the level and thickness of the obstruction change the operation. Here the ultrasound shows a normal uterus above a distended vagina and the membrane is directly visible at the introitus, and she has acute urinary retention that should not wait for imaging. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Hormonal suppression would stop further accumulation but leaves a large volume of retained blood under pressure, with continuing risk of retrograde flow into the peritoneal cavity and endometriosis. It does not relieve the urinary retention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Aspiration through the membrane leaves the obstruction in place so the collection reaccumulates, and it introduces organisms into a closed space filled with old blood, risking pyocolpos and ascending infection. Definitive incision is the treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Labial adhesions occur in a substantial minority of prepubertal girls, peaking between about three months and six years, and result from the physiologically low oestrogen state of childhood combined with minor local irritation causing the thin unoestrogenised labial edges to adhere. The appearance of a flat translucent avascular midline line distinguishes them from the congenital absence of an opening, and the urethral meatus remaining visible confirms the urinary outlet is unobstructed. The great majority resolve spontaneously, with essentially all having resolved by puberty as endogenous oestrogen rises. Treatment is therefore reserved for symptoms, which means urine pooling behind the fusion causing post-void dribbling, recurrent urinary tract infection, difficulty voiding or local discomfort, and the first line treatment is a short course of topical oestrogen applied along the line with gentle traction, with manual or surgical separation reserved for failure and recurrence after any separation common until puberty. A further consideration is that although adhesions themselves are not caused by abuse, any genital finding in a child prompts a general assessment for signs of trauma, which are absent here.
key_points: Fusion results from the low oestrogen state of childhood and resolves by puberty
A flat translucent midline line with a visible urethral meatus is the characteristic appearance
Treat only for symptoms such as post-void dribbling or recurrent infection
Topical oestrogen is first line when treatment is indicated
Forcible manual separation is painful, causes re-adhesion and is not recommended
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the child dribbles urine after leaving the toilet: post-void dribbling from urine pooling behind the fusion is the symptom that converts labial adhesions from a finding needing only reassurance into one needing topical oestrogen.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Forcible separation without anaesthesia is painful, causes bleeding and raw surfaces that frequently re-adhere more firmly, and is distressing in a way that affects future genital examinations. It is no longer recommended. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions)

Topical oestrogen is the correct first line treatment when the fusion causes symptoms, meaning urinary pooling with post-void dribbling, recurrent infection or difficulty voiding. Applied to an asymptomatic child it risks local irritation, breast budding and pigmentation for a condition that resolves on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions)

Midline fusion in a prepubertal girl arises from the low oestrogen state of childhood and resolves spontaneously as oestrogen rises at puberty, and often earlier. With a normal urinary stream, no post-void dribbling and no infections she is asymptomatic, so treatment carries risk without benefit and explanation to the mother is the intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions)

Surgical division is reserved for dense adhesions causing significant obstruction that have failed topical treatment. Exposing an asymptomatic 3-year-old to general anaesthesia for a self-limiting condition is not justified. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions)

Upper tract imaging is indicated where there is recurrent or atypical urinary infection or evidence of obstruction. She has a normal stream, is dry between voids, has never had an infection and has a negative urinalysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Actinomyces species are slow growing filamentous anaerobic bacteria that form part of the normal flora of the mouth and the gastrointestinal and genital tracts. They are identified on cervical cytology in a proportion of intrauterine device users that rises with duration of use, and the overwhelming majority of these women never develop any infection, so the finding represents colonisation rather than disease. This distinction has practical consequences, because historical practice of removing the device and prescribing antibiotics on the basis of a cytology comment caused unintended pregnancies and unnecessary antimicrobial exposure. Current Australian guidance is that an asymptomatic woman needs neither removal nor treatment, but should be advised of the symptoms that would warrant review, namely pelvic pain, fever, abnormal bleeding or altered discharge. Invasive pelvic actinomycosis is rare and presents as an indolent inflammatory mass that crosses tissue planes and can mimic malignancy, and it is treated with device removal and a prolonged course of high dose penicillin, typically intravenous initially and then oral over several months.
key_points: The cytology finding represents colonisation, not infection
Prevalence rises with duration of device use and most women never develop disease
Neither removal nor antibiotics are indicated in an asymptomatic woman
Advise review for pelvic pain, fever, abnormal bleeding or altered discharge
Invasive disease is rare, mimics malignancy and needs prolonged high dose penicillin
explanation.pearls: Invasive pelvic actinomycosis forms an inflammatory mass that crosses tissue planes and is repeatedly mistaken for ovarian malignancy at laparotomy, so it is worth considering in a long term device user with a pelvic mass before extensive resection is undertaken.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A short prophylactic course neither eradicates colonisation nor prevents invasive disease, and it contributes to antimicrobial resistance. There is no evidence supporting antibiotic prophylaxis for this finding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Removal on the basis of a cytology comment alone deprives her of a method she is satisfied with and exposes her to a risk of unintended pregnancy, without any evidence that it prevents subsequent infection. Removal is indicated only if pelvic infection develops. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Prolonged high dose penicillin is the treatment for established actinomycosis, a rare invasive infection with a pelvic mass, sinus formation and systemic features, which is why the regimen is recognisable. Applying it to asymptomatic colonisation exposes her to months of unnecessary antibiotics. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

These organisms are commensals of the genital tract found on cytology in a significant proportion of device users, and colonisation in an asymptomatic woman does not predict disease. Guidelines are explicit that neither removal nor antibiotic treatment is warranted where there are no symptoms and no signs of pelvic infection. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Imaging would be appropriate if she had pelvic pain, an adnexal mass or systemic features suggesting invasive disease. Investigating an asymptomatic woman with a normal examination generates incidental findings and anxiety without changing management. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer has no effective population screening test and presents late, with the commonest symptoms being abdominal bloating, early satiety, abdominal or pelvic pain, urinary urgency and a change in bowel habit. These are non-specific and are frequently attributed to irritable bowel syndrome, but new bowel type symptoms in a woman over 50 should prompt examination and investigation rather than a functional label. Assessment combines the woman's menopausal status, ultrasound appearances and CA125, and the features that raise concern are solid components, thick septations, bilateral disease, ascites and internal vascularity. CA125 must be interpreted with care because it is raised in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy, cirrhosis and heart failure, and it is normal in roughly half of early stage cancers, so a normal value never excludes disease in the presence of suspicious imaging.
