Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre before any surgery is the step most strongly associated with improved survival, because complete staging and optimal cytoreduction depend on the operating team, and inadvertent surgery elsewhere may upstage the disease through spillage.
key_points: Bloating, early satiety and altered bowel habit in a woman over 50 warrant examination and investigation
Solid components, thick septations, bilateral disease and ascites are the concerning features
CA125 is raised in many benign conditions and is normal in about half of early cancers
Refer before any surgery, because the operating team determines staging quality and survival
Cystectomy or laparoscopic surgery outside a specialist centre risks spillage and upstaging
explanation.pearls: A normal CA125 does not exclude ovarian cancer, since roughly half of stage one tumours have a value below 35 U/mL, so suspicious ultrasound appearances warrant specialist referral on imaging grounds alone.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A gastrointestinal primary metastasising to the ovaries is a genuine consideration given her altered bowel habit, and endoscopic assessment may well form part of the specialist workup. Arranging it first delays referral by weeks, and the specialist centre is better placed to sequence staging investigations. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

Interval imaging is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst under 5 cm with a normal CA125 in a postmenopausal woman. Applying surveillance to bilateral solid masses with ascites allows progression of a disease in which time to treatment matters. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This is the most consequential error available, because operating outside a specialist centre risks incomplete staging and rupture of the mass with spillage, both of which worsen outcome. Cystectomy is a conservative operation for a lesion presumed benign, which these appearances are not. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

Serial measurement is used for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, not for deciding whether an already suspicious mass warrants referral. A value of 480 U/mL alongside these imaging findings is sufficient on its own. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

Bilateral complex solid adnexal masses with ascites and a markedly raised CA125 in a postmenopausal woman indicate a high risk of malignancy. Surgery performed by a gynaecological oncologist in a specialist centre achieves better staging, higher rates of optimal cytoreduction and improved survival, so the referral itself is the intervention that changes outcome. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Perineal tears are graded by the structures involved: first degree involves skin or vaginal mucosa only, second degree extends into the perineal muscles, third degree involves the anal sphincter complex, and fourth degree extends through the anal epithelium. Third degree tears are subdivided into 3a with less than 50 per cent of the external sphincter torn, 3b with more than 50 per cent, and 3c with the internal sphincter also involved, and this grading matters because it guides repair technique and counselling about future births. Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are underdiagnosed unless a digital rectal examination is performed routinely after every vaginal birth, which is the specific practice that improves detection. Risk factors include first vaginal birth, birth weight above 4 kg, occipito posterior position, prolonged second stage and instrumental birth, particularly forceps. Repair is performed in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, with either overlap or end to end technique for the external sphincter and end to end for the internal sphincter, followed by broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy and structured follow up, since a proportion of women have persisting symptoms and will need counselling about the mode of a future birth.
key_points: Grade 3a is less than 50 per cent of the external sphincter, 3b more than 50 per cent, 3c includes the internal sphincter
Perform a digital rectal examination after every vaginal birth to detect these injuries
Repair in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, not under local infiltration
Birth weight above 4 kg, occipito posterior position and instrumental birth raise the risk
Follow up with antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and counselling about future births
explanation.pearls: Give a laxative rather than a constipating agent after obstetric anal sphincter repair, because straining against a hard stool disrupts the repair, and prescribe broad spectrum antibiotics at the time of repair to reduce wound breakdown.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Involvement of the external anal sphincter defines an obstetric anal sphincter injury, and these are repaired in an operating theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia, good lighting, proper instruments and an assistant. Anaesthesia relaxes the sphincter so the retracted torn ends can be retrieved and apposed, which is the single factor most associated with a sound repair and continence afterwards. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Local infiltration is appropriate for tears not involving the anal sphincter. It does not provide the muscle relaxation required to retrieve retracted sphincter ends, and repairs done this way are associated with higher rates of persisting defect and faecal incontinence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Leaving a torn sphincter unrepaired allows the ends to retract and fibrose, and secondary repair weeks later gives substantially worse functional results than primary repair. The window for primary repair is now. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Conservative management is reasonable for a superficial first degree tear that is haemostatic and well apposed. A sphincter injury left unrepaired carries a high risk of faecal urgency and incontinence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Colorectal involvement is valuable for complex or failed repairs and for later assessment of persisting symptoms. Primary repair of an acute obstetric sphincter injury is within the scope of an appropriately trained obstetrician and should not be delayed for a referral. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Australia screens every pregnant woman for hepatitis B surface antigen at booking, and a positive result triggers viral load and e antigen testing, liver function assessment, and referral for ongoing hepatitis care beyond the pregnancy. Vertical transmission is the dominant route of chronic infection worldwide, and infection acquired at birth carries a far higher risk of becoming chronic than infection acquired in adulthood, which is why prevention at this point matters so much. Every infant born to a positive mother receives hepatitis B immunoglobulin within twelve hours of birth together with the birth dose of vaccine, followed by the routine schedule. Maternal antiviral therapy is added above the viral load threshold and started in the late second or early third trimester, and is the measure that closes the residual failure rate of immunoprophylaxis. Serological testing of the infant at nine to twelve months confirms whether prophylaxis succeeded, and household contacts are screened and vaccinated.
key_points: Antiviral therapy is added when the maternal viral load exceeds 200 000 IU/mL
Treatment is started between 28 and 32 weeks, not at booking
Immunoglobulin plus vaccine within twelve hours of birth is given to every exposed infant
Caesarean birth does not reduce hepatitis B transmission
Breastfeeding is safe and encouraged once immunoprophylaxis has been given
explanation.pearls: Test the infant for surface antigen and surface antibody at nine to twelve months of age, well after the final vaccine dose, because testing earlier can detect passively acquired immunoglobulin antibody and give a falsely reassuring result.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis at birth is essential and prevents most transmission, but it fails in roughly one in ten infants when the maternal viral load is very high, which is the gap maternal antiviral therapy is designed to close. It is a necessary part of the plan rather than the whole of it. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Mode of birth has not been shown to reduce vertical transmission of hepatitis B when immunoprophylaxis is given, so caesarean exposes her to surgical risk without benefit. This contrasts with the situation in untreated maternal human immunodeficiency virus infection, where mode of birth does matter. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Breastfeeding is not a route of transmission once the infant has received immunoglobulin and vaccine, and it is actively encouraged in hepatitis B positive mothers including those taking tenofovir. Advising against it removes a benefit for no risk reduction. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Entecavir is an effective antiviral in non pregnant chronic hepatitis B but has far less safety data in pregnancy than the preferred agent, which has extensive exposure data from its use in pregnant women with human immunodeficiency virus. The choice of molecule, not the strategy, is what is wrong here. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Maternal antiviral therapy is recommended when the viral load exceeds 200 000 IU/mL, started between 28 and 32 weeks, because suppressing the load markedly reduces the residual transmission that immunoprophylaxis alone does not prevent. Tenofovir disoproxil is the preferred agent in pregnancy on the strength of its safety record and its high barrier to resistance. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

explanation.summary: Syphilis in pregnancy is screened for at booking across Australia, with repeat testing in the third trimester and at birth for women in higher prevalence settings or with ongoing risk, reflecting a sustained national rise in infectious syphilis and in congenital cases. A reactive treponemal test with a confirmatory assay establishes exposure, while the non treponemal titre measures activity and is the number followed to judge treatment response. Untreated maternal infection transmits to the fetus in a high proportion of cases and causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, rhinitis, bone lesions and later sensorineural deafness and dental abnormalities. Benzathine benzylpenicillin occupies a unique position because no alternative reliably treats the fetal compartment, which is why allergy is managed by desensitisation rather than by substitution. A fourfold fall in the non treponemal titre indicates successful treatment, and rising titres prompt reassessment for reinfection or failure.
key_points: Benzathine penicillin is the only agent proven to treat the fetus
Documented penicillin allergy in pregnancy is managed by desensitisation, not substitution
Doxycycline is contraindicated after the first trimester
Azithromycin fails because of resistance and poor placental transfer
A fourfold fall in the non treponemal titre defines treatment response
explanation.pearls: Warn the woman about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction, a fever, rigors and uterine contractions occurring within twelve to twenty four hours of the first penicillin dose, which in the second half of pregnancy warrants fetal monitoring because it can precipitate preterm labour and fetal distress.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because they deposit in developing teeth and bone, and this regimen has no established efficacy for preventing fetal infection. It is an acceptable alternative only outside pregnancy. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Ceftriaxone has some treponemal activity and is used in selected non pregnant situations, but the evidence for preventing congenital infection is inadequate and cross reactivity in a patient with true penicillin anaphylaxis is a further concern. The unique standing of penicillin here is that it is the only agent proven to treat the fetus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Benzathine benzylpenicillin is the only treatment shown to treat the fetus as well as the mother, so a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction is managed by desensitising under monitored conditions rather than by substituting another drug. Desensitisation is performed in a setting with resuscitation facilities and the penicillin is then given immediately afterwards. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin crosses the placenta poorly, so treatment failures with congenital infection have been repeatedly described. This is the option that most clearly fails the fetus while appearing to treat the mother. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Transmission rises steeply with gestation and untreated maternal infection causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth and congenital disease, so deferring guarantees the harm that treatment prevents. Treating the newborn afterwards does not undo damage sustained in utero. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes complicates a small proportion of pregnancies but precedes a third of preterm births, and management balances the risks of prematurity against those of ascending infection. Diagnosis is made on sterile speculum examination showing pooling, and digital examination is avoided because it shortens the latency period and introduces organisms. Standard management before 34 weeks is admission, antenatal corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, surveillance for chorioamnionitis with temperature, pulse, uterine tenderness, liquor colour and fetal heart rate, and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection when birth is imminent before 30 weeks. Expectant management continues to around 34 to 37 weeks depending on local protocol and on the appearance of any infective, abruption or fetal compromise trigger. Tocolysis is not routinely used because it does not improve neonatal outcome and may delay delivery in the presence of subclinical infection.
key_points: Sterile speculum confirms the diagnosis and digital examination is avoided
Erythromycin prolongs latency and reduces neonatal morbidity
Amoxicillin with clavulanate is avoided because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Corticosteroids are given, and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if birth is imminent before 30 weeks
Fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia or offensive liquor signal chorioamnionitis and mandate delivery
explanation.pearls: Latency antibiotics are given for a maximum of ten days and stopped once labour establishes, because prolonged courses select resistant organisms without further prolonging the pregnancy.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Intrapartum penicillin is the regimen for group B streptococcus prophylaxis and is given when a woman is colonised or her status is unknown, whereas her recent swab was negative. It also does nothing for the latency prolongation that is the aim in the antenatal period. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Erythromycin after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes prolongs the interval to birth, reduces neonatal infection, oxygen requirement and abnormal cerebral imaging, and is the regimen supported by the largest randomised evidence. Treatment stops at ten days or when labour begins, whichever comes first. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This combination also prolongs latency but was associated with a significant excess of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in the same trial that established the correct answer, so it is specifically avoided in this setting. The two arms differ in neonatal bowel outcome rather than in their effect on latency. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Anaerobic cover of this kind is used to treat established chorioamnionitis rather than to prolong latency in a woman with no clinical or biochemical signs of infection. Her normal temperature, soft uterus and near normal inflammatory markers place her in the latency group rather than the treatment group. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Waiting for clinical infection forgoes the demonstrated reduction in neonatal morbidity that prophylaxis achieves, and by the time chorioamnionitis is clinically apparent the fetus has usually already been exposed. Latency antibiotics are given to all women with preterm rupture, not only to those with signs. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed on two of three criteria, namely oligo or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Ultrasound morphology is not required when the first two criteria are both present, and it is not used at all within eight years of menarche because multifollicular ovaries are normal in that age group. Anovulation is the mechanism of subfertility, so treatment aims to restore ovulation rather than to bypass it. Lifestyle intervention is recommended for all women with a raised body mass index because even modest weight loss improves ovulatory function, but it is not a reason to delay pharmacological treatment in a woman who has already been trying for over a year. Before starting ovulation induction, tubal patency and semen analysis should be known, because inducing ovulation in the presence of an untreated tubal or male factor wastes cycles.
key_points: Two of three Rotterdam criteria establish the diagnosis after exclusions
Ultrasound is not required if anovulation and hyperandrogenism are both present
Letrozole is first line for ovulation induction and outperforms clomifene for live birth
Confirm tubal patency and semen analysis before inducing ovulation
Gonadotrophins and assisted reproduction follow failure of oral agents
explanation.pearls: Letrozole works by transiently lowering oestrogen and releasing the pituitary from negative feedback, which means it does not carry clomifene's antioestrogenic effect on endometrial thickness and cervical mucus, the mechanism behind clomifene's gap between ovulation and pregnancy rates.

sources.label: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Metformin improves ovulation rates modestly and is used as an adjunct or where the correct agent is unavailable or declined, but it is inferior to the recommended first line drug for live birth. Its main current place is in combination for women with a higher body mass index. (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.rationale: Gonadotrophins are second line for women who fail oral agents and require cycle monitoring because of the risks of multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation. Using them before an oral agent has been tried exposes her to those risks unnecessarily. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Assisted reproduction is reserved for failure of ovulation induction or for a coexisting tubal or male factor, neither of which applies given patent tubes and two normal semen analyses. Most anovulatory women conceive with a simple oral agent at a fraction of the cost and risk. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Clomifene was the long standing first line agent and remains effective, but head to head trials show the correct answer achieves higher ovulation, clinical pregnancy and live birth rates in this population. The difference lies in clomifene's antioestrogenic effect on the endometrium and cervical mucus, which the alternative avoids. (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.rationale: Letrozole is the recommended first line agent for ovulation induction in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome, producing higher live birth rates than clomifene without the antioestrogenic endometrial effect. Confirming ovulation with a mid luteal progesterone before escalating the dose is what makes the treatment a controlled sequence rather than a guess. (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception in Australia comprises two oral options and the copper intrauterine device, and choosing between them depends on time since intercourse, position in the cycle, body weight, current hormonal contraception and what ongoing method the woman wants. Levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours and ulipristal up to 120 hours, while the copper device may be inserted up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation, whichever is later. Both oral agents act by delaying or preventing ovulation and therefore fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, which means effectiveness falls precisely in the fertile window where risk is greatest. The copper device has an additional post fertilisation mechanism, which is why its failure rate is under one per cent regardless of cycle timing or body weight. Ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator, so hormonal contraception is delayed for five days after taking it and additional precautions are needed until the new method is reliable.
key_points: The copper device is the most effective option and is unaffected by weight or cycle timing
Oral agents act by delaying ovulation and fail once the surge has started
Levonorgestrel efficacy declines above about seventy kilograms
Ulipristal extends the window to 120 hours but is also weight sensitive
Hormonal contraception is delayed for five days after ulipristal
explanation.pearls: Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhoea at the time of emergency device insertion but do not delay the insertion waiting for results, because the pregnancy risk is immediate while any detected infection can be treated with the device left in place.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: The copper device is the most effective emergency contraceptive, with a failure rate under one per cent, and unlike the oral options its efficacy is unaffected by body weight or by how close ovulation is, because it prevents implantation as well as fertilisation. It also answers her request for ongoing contraception in the same procedure. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Levonorgestrel works only by delaying ovulation, so it is least effective at exactly the point in the cycle when the risk is highest, and its efficacy declines above about seventy kilograms. Both of the factors that reduce its effectiveness are present in her case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Ulipristal delays ovulation later in the follicular phase than levonorgestrel does and is the better oral choice here, but its efficacy also falls with increasing body weight above about eighty five kilograms and it still cannot act once the luteinising hormone surge has peaked. It is the correct oral option and remains less effective than the device. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Doubling the dose is sometimes offered where no better option exists, but the evidence that it restores efficacy at higher body weight is weak and no pregnancy outcome benefit has been demonstrated. It is a workaround rather than a solution when a device is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Starting ongoing contraception is appropriate but a combined pill begun after the exposure provides no emergency cover for intercourse that has already occurred. It also cannot be started immediately after ulipristal without reducing that drug's effect. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

explanation.summary: Around three quarters of women who labour after one previous lower segment caesarean achieve a vaginal birth, and the background risk of uterine rupture in spontaneous labour is roughly one in two hundred. That risk rises with induction and augmentation, and the rise is steepest with prostaglandin agents, which is why mechanical ripening has become the preferred approach when the cervix is unfavourable. Contraindications to attempting vaginal birth include a previous classical or inverted T incision, previous uterine rupture, a placenta praevia or accreta, and any other standard indication for caesarean. The practical requirements for a trial of labour are a hospital with immediate access to theatre and blood, continuous electronic fetal monitoring in established labour, and intravenous access. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign of scar rupture and precedes scar pain, loss of contractions, vaginal bleeding and maternal haemodynamic change.
key_points: Uterine rupture risk in spontaneous labour after one caesarean is about one in two hundred
Prostaglandin ripening approximately doubles that risk and misoprostol is contraindicated
Mechanical balloon ripening is preferred for an unfavourable cervix
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is required in established labour
An abnormal fetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar rupture
explanation.pearls: Two or more previous caesareans, a short interdelivery interval of under eighteen months, and induction of labour each independently raise rupture risk, and it is the combination rather than any single factor that most often tips counselling toward a repeat caesarean.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Mechanical ripening with a balloon catheter avoids the excess uterine rupture risk associated with prostaglandin ripening in a scarred uterus while still converting an unfavourable cervix, and it is the preferred method in Australian practice for this situation. Continuous electronic fetal monitoring follows once labour is established because an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar dehiscence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Prostaglandin ripening roughly doubles the risk of uterine rupture compared with spontaneous labour in a woman with a previous caesarean, and that risk is the reason mechanical methods are preferred. The two approaches achieve similar cervical change, so the difference is entirely one of scar safety. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Misoprostol carries the highest rupture risk of all ripening agents in a scarred uterus and is contraindicated for induction at term after a previous caesarean. Its use in obstetrics at term is confined to women with no uterine scar. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

Artificial rupture of membranes is not feasible with a closed, firm, posterior cervix at station minus three, and oxytocin without cervical ripening in this setting produces a prolonged induction with a high failure rate. The unfavourable Bishop score is what makes a ripening step necessary first. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A repeat caesarean is a legitimate choice and must remain available to her, but an unfavourable cervix alone is not a contraindication to induction, and abandoning her stated preference without offering a safe ripening method is not supported. This would be the answer if she changed her mind or if a contraindication to labour emerged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Maternal thyroxine requirement rises early in pregnancy because oestrogen driven thyroxine binding globulin increases, human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the gland, placental deiodinase increases hormone degradation, and the plasma volume expands. Women with an intact gland accommodate this automatically, whereas women on replacement cannot and need their dose increased. The fetal thyroid does not begin producing hormone until around twelve weeks, so the whole of early neurodevelopment depends on transplacental maternal thyroxine, which is why the increase is made immediately rather than at the first antenatal visit. The recommended first trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L, and levels are rechecked every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy and at least once thereafter. Iron, calcium and antacids, all common in pregnancy, bind levothyroxine in the gut and must be separated from it by at least four hours, which is a frequent and easily missed cause of apparent dose failure.
key_points: Requirement rises by roughly 25 to 30 per cent in the first trimester
Two extra tablets per week delivers approximately that increase without a new prescription
First trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L
The fetal thyroid does not function until about twelve weeks
Iron and calcium must be taken at least four hours apart from levothyroxine
explanation.pearls: Recheck thyroid function four weeks after any dose change and then every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy, and return to the pre-pregnancy dose immediately after birth with a further check six weeks postpartum.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Thyroid hormone requirement rises from very early in the first trimester, so holding the dose steady for seven weeks leaves her underdosed during the period when fetal brain development depends entirely on maternal hormone. A pre-pregnancy level of 2.0 does not provide a margin large enough to absorb that rise. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Requirement increases by roughly a quarter to a third within the first weeks, and adding two extra tablets each week delivers about that increase immediately using the tablets she already has. Rechecking in four weeks then confirms the first trimester target has been reached rather than assumed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Testing is certainly needed, but waiting several days for the result before acting delays an increase that is predictable in every treated hypothyroid pregnancy, so the dose is raised at the same time the test is ordered. This is one of the few situations where empirical dose adjustment precedes the result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

The transient fall in thyroid stimulating hormone seen in early pregnancy reflects stimulation of the thyroid by human chorionic gonadotropin in women with a functioning gland, which she does not have. In treated hypothyroidism the requirement rises rather than falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Combination therapy with triiodothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta poorly and suppresses maternal thyroid stimulating hormone without supplying the thyroxine the fetus needs. Levothyroxine alone is the only appropriate replacement in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiseizure medications, with major congenital malformations in roughly one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment, reduced cognitive scores and increased autism spectrum diagnoses in a substantially larger proportion. Both risks are dose dependent, and there is no dose that has been shown to be free of neurodevelopmental effect. Australian regulatory advice requires that valproate is not used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, that effective contraception is in place, and that the risks are discussed and documented at least annually. Preconception is the only safe point at which to change treatment, because a switch made after a positive pregnancy test exposes the fetus during organogenesis to both the old and the new drug. Where valproate genuinely cannot be replaced, the dose is minimised, the daily dose is divided, high dose folate is given, and the pregnancy is managed jointly by neurology and obstetrics.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformations in about ten per cent and neurodevelopmental harm in more
Both effects are dose dependent and folate does not offset them
Any switch is completed and stability confirmed before conception
Contraception is maintained until the new regimen is established
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and loss of driving privileges
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises substantially through pregnancy because of oestrogen induced glucuronidation, so levels fall and doses often need increasing, then must be reduced promptly within days of birth to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: High dose folate is recommended for any woman with epilepsy planning pregnancy, but it does not offset the dose-dependent risk of neural tube defects, other major malformations and impaired childhood neurodevelopment that valproate carries. Adding folate without changing the drug gives the appearance of mitigation without the substance of it. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.rationale: Detailed anomaly imaging will detect structural defects but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental and autism spectrum outcomes that constitute the largest part of the harm, and by then the exposure has already occurred. Surveillance is not a substitute for avoiding the exposure. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A supervised switch to an agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam must be completed and stability confirmed before conception, because changing during an established pregnancy exposes the fetus to both drugs and risks breakthrough seizures. Referring now, while she still has effective contraception in place, is what creates the time the switch requires. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic clonic seizures risks status epilepticus, loss of her driver licence and injury, and maternal seizures in pregnancy carry their own fetal risks including hypoxia and trauma. Any change is a supervised cross titration rather than a cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Switching an antiseizure medication in a woman with generalised epilepsy is specialist work, and carbamazepine can aggravate generalised seizure types including absence and myoclonic seizures as well as carrying its own teratogenic risk. The specific hazard here is choosing an agent that is wrong for her seizure syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets constitute a severe variant of pre-eclampsia that can present with only modest hypertension and minimal proteinuria, so severity is judged on the end-organ picture rather than on the blood pressure reading. Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain from hepatic capsular distension is the characteristic symptom and is often misattributed to reflux, gallbladder disease or gastroenteritis, which delays diagnosis. The main differential is acute fatty liver of pregnancy, which is distinguished by hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with a prolonged international normalised ratio, a rising creatinine and often encephalopathy, none of which is present here. Complications include eclampsia, placental abruption, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and hepatic haematoma or rupture, and the disease may worsen for the first twenty four to forty eight hours after birth, so postnatal surveillance continues. Birth is the only definitive treatment, and the decision to deliver is made on the maternal condition rather than on the gestation once past thirty four weeks.
key_points: Blood pressure may be only mildly raised and proteinuria minimal
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain reflects hepatic capsular stretch
Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and rising creatinine suggest acute fatty liver instead
Birth is the only definitive treatment and is not deferred past 34 weeks
The disease can worsen in the first two days after birth
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and continued for twenty four hours after birth, with monitoring of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output, and calcium gluconate kept immediately available as the antidote for toxicity.

sources.label: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Platelets are consumed rapidly in this process so a transfusion given without delivering produces only a transient rise, and it is reserved for active bleeding or for cover immediately before an operative procedure. Transfusing to defer the decision treats the number rather than the disease. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

Expectant management is considered only before 34 weeks and only where maternal and fetal parameters are stable, whereas she is past 34 weeks with an actively deteriorating haematological and hepatic picture. The syndrome characteristically progresses over hours rather than days. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Corticosteroids do produce a transient improvement in platelet count but have not been shown to improve maternal or perinatal outcome, and using them to justify prolonging the pregnancy is the error rather than the drug itself. Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are a separate and legitimate indication. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Haemolysis with fragmented cells, transaminases above twice the upper limit and platelets below 100 x10^9/L at 34 weeks establishes a severe manifestation of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in which the only definitive treatment is birth. Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and the blood pressure treated while delivery is organised. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Lowering the blood pressure prevents maternal stroke but does nothing to halt the underlying endothelial and hepatic process, so treating the pressure alone and sending her home would allow the syndrome to progress unobserved. Her pressure is also not in the severe range, which is precisely why it cannot be used to gauge severity here. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with a mechanical heart valve is one of the highest risk cardiac situations in obstetrics, and no anticoagulation strategy is free of harm, so the task is to choose the least bad option for the individual woman and to document the discussion. Warfarin gives the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between six and twelve weeks, together with fetal intracranial haemorrhage later in pregnancy. That embryopathy risk is dose dependent, and the widely used threshold is a daily requirement of 5 mg or less, below which continuation through the first trimester is considered reasonable and above which a switch to low molecular weight heparin between six and twelve weeks is preferred. Heparins do not cross the placenta and so carry no fetal risk, but they protect the valve less reliably and demand twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment. Mitral position, older generation prostheses, atrial fibrillation and a previous thromboembolic event all raise thrombotic risk and push the balance back toward warfarin.
key_points: No regimen is risk free; the choice is documented shared decision making
Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent, with 5 mg daily as the usual threshold
The vulnerable window for embryopathy is six to twelve weeks
Low molecular weight heparin requires twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve
explanation.pearls: Warfarin is converted to intravenous unfractionated heparin at around thirty six weeks and the heparin stopped four to six hours before birth, because a warfarinised fetus has an anticoagulated brain and vaginal birth then carries an unacceptable risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves at any time because a randomised trial in non pregnant patients was stopped early for excess valve thrombosis and stroke, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. This is the one option that is wrong on both counts simultaneously. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Pregnancy is a strongly prothrombotic state and a mechanical mitral prosthesis left unanticoagulated for six weeks carries a high risk of valve thrombosis, which is frequently fatal to both mother and fetus. Her missed doses and an international normalised ratio already down at 1.6 make this the immediate danger rather than a theoretical one. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin is a legitimate first trimester strategy and the one chosen when the warfarin requirement is high, but it must be given twice daily with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment, because valve thrombosis has occurred in pregnant women dosed on weight without monitoring. The flaw is the omission of monitoring rather than the choice of drug. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin carries the highest rate of valve thrombosis of all the regimens used in this setting and commits her to hospital or to an indwelling line for six weeks with attendant infection and osteoporosis risk. Its proper place is the immediate peripartum window, not the first trimester. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose dependent and is low when the daily requirement is 5 mg or less, so continuing warfarin through the first trimester carries the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis and an acceptable fetal risk at her dose of 4 mg. Her subtherapeutic ratio of 1.6 makes restoration urgent, and the decision is made with her after explicit counselling because both branches carry real risk. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis arises from milk stasis with or without bacterial infection, and in this woman both elements are present: she has been feeding predominantly on the right because of pain, and a nipple fissure has given Staphylococcus aureus a portal of entry. The counterintuitive but essential instruction is to keep feeding from the affected breast, because continued milk removal resolves the stasis that sustains the inflammation, and the milk is safe for the baby. Antibiotics are indicated when systemic features persist beyond about 24 hours, when there is a nipple fissure, or when conservative measures fail, and flucloxacillin is the appropriate choice. Failure to improve within 48 hours, or a discrete fluctuant mass, suggests abscess and requires ultrasound with aspiration or drainage. Addressing attachment is what prevents recurrence.
key_points: Milk stasis is the underlying mechanism, so continued effective milk removal is central to treatment.
Breastfeeding from the affected side is safe for the baby and should continue.
Flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, the usual organism entering through a nipple fissure.
Failure to improve within 48 hours or a fluctuant mass suggests abscess requiring ultrasound and drainage.
Review of attachment and positioning addresses the cause and prevents recurrence.
explanation.pearls: Tell a woman with mastitis to feed more often from the affected breast rather than less, because stopping feeds on that side is the commonest reason simple mastitis progresses to an abscess, and review her attachment to fix the fissure that let the organism in.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.rationale: Stopping removal of milk from an inflamed segment worsens stasis, which is the mechanism driving the inflammation, and markedly increases the likelihood of progression to abscess. Suppression also ends breastfeeding for a problem that resolves with treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.rationale: Ultrasound with drainage is the pathway once an abscess has formed, indicated by a fluctuant or discrete tender mass or by failure to improve after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. She has diffuse segmental firmness without a discrete or fluctuant mass, so she has not reached that point. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.rationale: Conservative management with improved milk removal is appropriate for blocked ducts and for inflammation of under 24 hours without systemic features. Thirty six hours of fever at 38.6 degrees C with tachycardia and a fissured nipple providing a portal of entry indicates infection that needs antibiotic treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and does not cover Staphylococcus aureus, which is the usual pathogen entering through a nipple fissure. Discarding expressed milk is also unnecessary, since the milk is safe for the baby and continued feeding is part of the treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.rationale: Effective and frequent milk removal from the affected side is the central treatment because stasis drives the inflammation, and continued feeding poses no risk to the baby. Flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, which enters through the nipple fissure, and referral for attachment review addresses the cracked nipple and the underfeeding of that breast that together caused the problem. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia complicates around one in ten pregnancies and gestational thrombocytopenia accounts for the large majority of cases. Its defining features are a normal count in early pregnancy with a gradual third trimester fall, an asymptomatic woman, a count that rarely drops below 70 x10^9/L, and resolution within weeks of delivery. The differential is separated on the history and the accompanying results rather than on the platelet count alone: immune thrombocytopenia typically predates the pregnancy or presents earlier and falls further, while pre-eclampsia and the HELLP syndrome bring hypertension, proteinuria, raised transaminases and red cell fragments. No treatment is required and the count should simply be monitored to delivery. Most anaesthetists will site a neuraxial block above about 70 to 80 x10^9/L provided the count is stable and there is no coagulopathy.
key_points: Gestational thrombocytopenia causes a gradual third trimester fall in a previously normal count.
It is asymptomatic, rarely falls below 70 x10^9/L, and resolves within weeks of delivery.
Immune thrombocytopenia usually predates pregnancy or appears earlier and falls further.
Hypertension, proteinuria, raised transaminases or red cell fragments point to pre-eclampsia or the HELLP syndrome.
Neuraxial anaesthesia is generally acceptable above a stable count of about 70 to 80 x10^9/L.
explanation.pearls: Look at the booking platelet count before working up thrombocytopenia in late pregnancy, because a normal count in the first trimester that drifts down in the third is gestational and needs nothing, whereas a count that was already low points to immune thrombocytopenia and changes the management entirely.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Corticosteroid is the first line treatment for immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy, which is suggested by a count that was already low before pregnancy or in the first trimester, or by a fall below about 75 x10^9/L. Her count was normal at booking and has fallen gradually in the third trimester, which is the opposite pattern. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

Immunoglobulin raises the count rapidly and is reserved for immune thrombocytopenia with bleeding or with very low counts close to delivery, where a fast response is needed. Using it for a physiological process in an asymptomatic woman exposes her to a blood product without any indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

A count that was normal at booking and has drifted down only in the third trimester, in a well woman with no bleeding, normal blood pressure, normal liver enzymes and a normal film, is gestational thrombocytopenia, which accounts for the great majority of low platelet counts in pregnancy and requires no treatment. Serial monitoring is all that is needed, and a count above 70 to 80 x10^9/L generally permits neuraxial anaesthesia, which is the question she is actually asking. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

Delivery is the treatment for the HELLP syndrome, in which thrombocytopenia occurs alongside haemolysis and raised transaminases, usually with hypertension and epigastric pain. Her liver enzymes are normal, her blood pressure is normal, her film shows no fragments and she has no symptoms, which excludes it. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

Platelet transfusion is reserved for active bleeding or for counts well below the threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia at the time of delivery. Transfusing prophylactically at 98 x10^9/L would give a short lived rise, risk alloimmunisation and treat a number rather than a problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Thyroxine requirements increase from the earliest weeks of pregnancy because oestrogen raises thyroxine binding globulin, the placenta degrades maternal hormone, and human chorionic gonadotrophin alters the set point. The fetal thyroid does not produce hormone until around 12 weeks, so first trimester brain development depends entirely on maternal thyroxine. A thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.9 mIU/L that was acceptable outside pregnancy sits above the first trimester target of 2.5 mIU/L. The correct action is therefore to increase the dose immediately on confirmation of pregnancy rather than waiting for a new result, then monitor four to six weekly. The multivitamin is a second correctable problem, because iron and calcium chelate levothyroxine and substantially reduce absorption.
key_points: Levothyroxine requirements rise by roughly 25 to 50 percent from the first trimester of pregnancy.
Dose is increased as soon as pregnancy is confirmed rather than waiting for a new thyroid result.
The first trimester thyroid stimulating hormone target is below 2.5 mIU/L in treated hypothyroidism.
Iron and calcium reduce levothyroxine absorption and must be separated by at least four hours.
Liothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta poorly while suppressing maternal thyroid stimulating hormone.
explanation.pearls: Tell every woman on levothyroxine who is planning pregnancy to take two extra tablets each week from the day her test is positive and to telephone for a thyroid function test, because waiting for the appointment costs several weeks of the period when fetal brain development depends wholly on maternal supply.

options.rationale: Continuing unchanged would be right if thyroid requirements were stable in pregnancy, and they rise by roughly a quarter to a half from very early gestation as binding globulin increases and the placenta deiodinates hormone. Deferring the first check to 20 weeks misses the first trimester, when fetal brain development depends entirely on maternal supply. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

Withdrawal would be considered where replacement had been started without a confirmed diagnosis, and this woman has antibody positive autoimmune hypothyroidism requiring lifelong treatment. Stopping would produce overt maternal hypothyroidism during organogenesis, which is associated with pregnancy loss and impaired neurodevelopment. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

Combination therapy with triiodothyronine is occasionally trialled in non pregnant patients with persistent symptoms despite normal biochemistry, and it is specifically avoided in pregnancy. Triiodothyronine crosses the placenta poorly and suppresses maternal thyroid stimulating hormone without supplying the fetus with the thyroxine it needs. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

Requirements rise from early in the first trimester, so the accepted practice is to increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed rather than waiting for a result, commonly by taking two additional tablets each week, with thyroid function checked within four weeks and then four to six weekly against a first trimester target below 2.5 mIU/L. Taking levothyroxine with iron and calcium markedly reduces its absorption, so separating them by at least four hours is part of the same correction. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

Free triiodothyronine is useful in assessing thyrotoxicosis, particularly the triiodothyronine predominant form, and it is not used to titrate replacement. Thyroid stimulating hormone with free thyroxine against trimester specific ranges is the correct monitoring pair in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: A complete hydatidiform mole arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material, giving a diploid conceptus of entirely paternal origin with no fetal tissue, which matches the histology and the ultrasound appearance here. Presentation with bleeding, a uterus large for dates, hyperemesis and a very high human chorionic gonadotrophin is characteristic, and thyrotoxicosis can occur because the hormone cross reacts with the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor. After suction evacuation the central task is surveillance, because approximately one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is detected by a hormone level that plateaus or rises rather than falling to normal. Reliable contraception throughout follow up is essential, since a new pregnancy would make the hormone uninterpretable and mask progression. Registration with a trophoblast centre and adherence to the surveillance schedule are what make this a highly curable condition.
key_points: A complete mole is diploid and entirely paternal in origin, with no fetal tissue present.
A uterus large for dates, hyperemesis and a very high hormone level are characteristic features.
Around one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
Progression is detected by a hormone level that plateaus or rises rather than normalising.
Reliable contraception is essential throughout follow up so that the hormone remains interpretable.
explanation.pearls: Stress that contraception is part of the treatment rather than an optional extra after a molar pregnancy, because a new pregnancy raises human chorionic gonadotrophin and makes it impossible to distinguish a healthy conception from the trophoblastic neoplasia that follows about one in six complete moles.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Gestational trophoblastic disease

options.rationale: Chemotherapy is given for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is diagnosed when the hormone plateaus or rises across defined measurements, when it remains detectable beyond six months, or when metastases or choriocarcinoma histology are present. A level falling from 268 000 to 4 100 IU/L over two weeks is the expected decline after successful evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

A second evacuation is considered for persistent heavy bleeding or ultrasound evidence of substantial retained tissue, and it carries risks of perforation and intrauterine adhesions. Her bleeding has settled and her hormone level is falling appropriately, so there is nothing to suggest retained tissue. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

Surveillance exists because around one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and that progression is detected only by a hormone level that plateaus or rises, so the measurement must not be confounded. Pregnancy would raise the hormone and make the result uninterpretable, which is why effective contraception is essential throughout follow up, and the combined oral contraceptive pill is acceptable once the level has normalised. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

Discharging her would forfeit the entire purpose of managing molar pregnancy, since the risk that matters arises after the evacuation rather than before it. Progression to neoplasia is curable when detected by surveillance and considerably more dangerous when it presents late with metastatic disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

Hysterectomy is an option for women who have completed their family, particularly those over 40 or with heavy bleeding, and it reduces but does not eliminate the risk of neoplasia because metastatic disease can still occur. Recommending it to a 31-year-old who wants another pregnancy would be disproportionate. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

explanation.summary: The distinction that determines management in genital herpes in pregnancy is whether the episode is a primary infection or a recurrence, and clinical appearance alone cannot make it because a first clinical episode may be the first recognised recurrence of a long standing infection. Type specific serology resolves this: antibodies absent alongside a positive swab confirms true primary infection. That matters because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the neonate, so a woman with recurrent disease transmits in fewer than three percent of vaginal births, whereas primary infection within six weeks of delivery carries a transmission risk approaching forty percent. Primary infection in the third trimester is therefore treated with aciclovir continued as suppression, and caesarean section is offered, ideally before membranes rupture. Serial antenatal viral cultures were abandoned because they predict shedding at delivery poorly.
key_points: Type specific serology distinguishes true primary infection from a first recognised recurrence.
Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the neonate, which recurrent disease provides and primary does not.
Primary infection within six weeks of delivery carries transmission risk approaching forty percent.
Recurrent disease carries a transmission risk below three percent and permits vaginal birth.
Serial antenatal viral cultures predict shedding at delivery poorly and are no longer performed.
explanation.pearls: Send type specific serology alongside the swab in any first episode of genital herpes in pregnancy, because absent antibodies confirm primary infection and change the plan from vaginal birth to caesarean section, while a positive antibody result means this is a recurrence and vaginal birth remains appropriate.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Vaginal birth with maternal antiviral cover is reasonable for recurrent disease, where transplacental antibody protects the neonate and transmission risk is low. Intrapartum aciclovir does not reduce neonatal transmission in a woman who has no antibodies to pass on. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

Topical antiviral treatment is ineffective for genital herpes and systemic treatment is required. Deferring the decision to labour also removes the opportunity to plan a birth that avoids contact with the infected genital tract at the time transmission occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

Serial antenatal cultures were used historically and were abandoned because they predict shedding at delivery poorly, with negative swabs frequently followed by shedding in labour. Basing the mode of birth on them would give false reassurance. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

Negative type specific serology alongside a positive swab confirms a genuine primary infection, meaning she has not yet developed antibodies to transfer across the placenta, and neonatal transmission risk during vaginal birth approaches forty percent when primary infection occurs within six weeks of delivery. Aciclovir treats the episode and is continued as suppression until birth, while caesarean section performed before membrane rupture avoids the exposure that causes neonatal herpes, a condition with high mortality and neurological morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

Neonatal aciclovir is treatment for established or strongly suspected neonatal infection rather than a substitute for avoiding exposure. Neonatal herpes carries substantial mortality and neurological morbidity even when treated, so prevention at the time of birth is far preferable. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of pregnant women with asthma deteriorate during pregnancy, and self reduction of preventer medication out of concern for the fetus is one of the commonest reasons. The evidence is consistent that inhaled corticosteroids are safe in pregnancy while poorly controlled asthma is not, because maternal hypoxaemia is associated with fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, pre-eclampsia and perinatal mortality. This woman has clear markers of loss of control: daily reliever use, night waking and a peak flow at two thirds of her personal best. The correct response is to restore the dose that previously worked and review early to confirm the response. Explaining why the medication is safer than the disease is what prevents the same reduction happening again.
key_points: Inhaled corticosteroids are safe in pregnancy and should be continued at the dose that maintains control.
Uncontrolled asthma causes fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and perinatal mortality.
Night waking, daily reliever use and a peak flow below 80 percent of personal best all indicate poor control.
Oral corticosteroid is used for acute exacerbations in pregnancy and should not be withheld when indicated.
Asthma control should be reviewed at every antenatal visit and a written action plan provided.
explanation.pearls: Ask every pregnant woman with asthma whether she has changed her own dose since the pregnancy test, because self reduction of inhaled corticosteroid is the commonest cause of second trimester deterioration and is corrected by restoring the previous dose with a review inside two weeks.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids have a long record of safe use in pregnancy and the risk to the fetus comes from uncontrolled asthma rather than from the medication, because maternal hypoxaemia causes growth restriction, preterm birth and perinatal loss. Returning to the dose that previously achieved control, with an early review to confirm it has worked, directly addresses the cause of her deterioration. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Reliever only treatment is not an accepted strategy for persistent asthma at any time, and it would accelerate exactly the deterioration she is already showing. Escalating short-acting beta agonist use is a marker of poor control rather than a treatment for it. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Montelukast can be continued in pregnancy in women already established on it and stabilised by it, but it is a weaker controller than inhaled corticosteroid and is not a substitute for the dose she has withdrawn. Substituting it also leaves her original misconception about steroid safety uncorrected. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid is used for acute exacerbations and is given in pregnancy when indicated, but this woman is not acutely exacerbating and is speaking in full sentences with normal oxygen saturation. Systemic steroid without restoring the preventer treats the symptom and leaves the cause in place. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Investigation would be warranted if the diagnosis were uncertain or an alternative cause such as infection or embolism were suspected, and here the history explains the deterioration completely. Delaying treatment for tests postpones the correction of a problem you have already identified. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is infarction of the anterior pituitary caused by hypotension from major obstetric haemorrhage, occurring because the gland enlarges during pregnancy and outgrows its low pressure portal blood supply. The earliest and most characteristic clinical clue is failure of lactation, since prolactin secreting cells are affected, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and loss of axillary and pubic hair. The biochemical signature is deficiency across several axes with inappropriately low or normal trophic hormones, and the key interpretive point is that a low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone is a pituitary result rather than a normal one. Hyponatraemia from glucocorticoid deficiency is common. Hydrocortisone must be replaced before thyroxine, because thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in an unreplaced patient.
key_points: Failure of lactation after major obstetric haemorrhage is the earliest clue to pituitary infarction.
A low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates pituitary rather than thyroid failure.
An undetectable prolactin in the postnatal period is strongly abnormal and supports the diagnosis.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium reflects glucocorticoid deficiency with preserved mineralocorticoid function.
Glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Always give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine when replacing multiple pituitary hormones, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and raises metabolic demand, and starting it first in an unreplaced patient can precipitate a fatal adrenal crisis within days.

options.rationale: A low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal thyroid stimulating hormone, an undetectable prolactin and a low 9 am cortisol together indicate panhypopituitarism, which in this context follows ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary after major obstetric haemorrhage. The order matters critically, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and giving it before glucocorticoid replacement can precipitate an adrenal crisis, and imaging then confirms the empty or shrunken gland. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Thyroxine replacement is indeed needed, and starting it before glucocorticoid in a patient with unrecognised adrenal insufficiency increases metabolic demand and cortisol clearance and can precipitate a life threatening crisis. The sequence rather than the drug is the error. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Postnatal fatigue and lactational amenorrhoea are extremely common and would be the right interpretation in a woman who is breastfeeding and otherwise well. Failure of lactation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and loss of secondary sexual hair are not features of normal recovery. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Oestrogen replacement is part of long term management of the gonadotrophin deficiency and addresses only one of several failing axes. Prescribing it alone would produce withdrawal bleeds while leaving untreated the cortisol and thyroxine deficiencies that are making her unwell and putting her at risk. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Postpartum thyroiditis is common and causes a hypothyroid phase within the first year, and it produces a raised thyroid stimulating hormone because the pituitary responds normally to a failing thyroid. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal with a low free thyroxine, which localises the problem to the pituitary. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis producing pallor, thinning and crinkling of vulval skin with architectural loss including resorption of the labia minora and introital narrowing. It is controlled rather than cured with ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, and long term maintenance treatment reduces both symptoms and the risk of malignant transformation. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around four to five percent, and malignancy characteristically arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is not associated with human papillomavirus and occurs in older women on a background of lichen sclerosus. The warning signs are a localised thickened, indurated, ulcerated or eroded area, or failure to respond to previously effective treatment. Any such area requires biopsy of the abnormal site rather than escalation of topical therapy or clinical observation.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus causes pallor, thinning, crinkling and architectural loss with introital narrowing.
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is about four to five percent.
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia arises on lichen sclerosus and is not related to human papillomavirus.
Induration, ulceration or failure to respond to previously effective corticosteroid mandates biopsy.
Long term maintenance topical corticosteroid reduces symptoms, architectural damage and cancer risk.
explanation.pearls: Biopsy any area of lichen sclerosus that stops responding to a corticosteroid that previously worked, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia cannot be distinguished clinically from a hypertrophic plaque and is the route by which around one in twenty of these women develop squamous cell carcinoma.

options.rationale: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are second line agents for lichen sclerosus that has not responded to corticosteroid, and using one here would treat a lesion that has not been characterised. Three months of a further topical agent delays the histological answer that a non responding indurated area demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma of around four to five percent, and the transition is heralded by exactly this change: a localised area that becomes thickened, indurated, ulcerated or fails to respond to treatment that previously worked. Biopsy of the specific abnormal area, rather than of unaffected skin, is the only way to distinguish differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or an early carcinoma from hypertrophic lichen sclerosus. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

Hypertrophic or thickened plaques do occur within lichen sclerosus and cannot be distinguished clinically from differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or early invasion, which is why they are biopsied rather than observed. Six months of review would allow an early carcinoma to progress to nodal disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

Cross sectional imaging stages disease once malignancy has been confirmed histologically and defines nodal involvement before surgery. Performed before any tissue diagnosis it cannot distinguish a benign plaque from a malignant one, because that distinction is cellular rather than anatomical. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

Wide excision is the treatment for confirmed neoplasia and its extent is determined by the histology and margins required, so operating before diagnosis risks both inadequate and unnecessarily mutilating surgery. Excising all lichen sclerosus affected skin would also be disfiguring and would not prevent recurrence elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: The critical skill in this scenario is recognising that caput and moulding make the vaginal station misleading, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable guide to descent. Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally with 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding means the true station is higher than the spines suggests, placing this in mid cavity territory with an occipitotransverse position.
