Instrumental birth in these circumstances has a meaningfully higher failure rate, which is why the attempt belongs in theatre as a trial with the team prepared to proceed immediately to caesarean section. Non rotational forceps are excluded by the transverse position. The cardiotocograph does not meet category one criteria, so there is time to move the woman and prepare properly.
key_points: Caput and moulding falsely lower the apparent station, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable measure of descent.
More than one fifth of the head palpable abdominally makes instrumental birth substantially more likely to fail.
Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position and are contraindicated in a transverse position.
A trial of instrumental birth in theatre allows immediate recourse to caesarean section without a second attempt.
Category one caesarean requires immediate threat to life, which normal variability with recovering variables does not meet.
explanation.pearls: Palpate the abdomen before every instrumental birth and treat more than one fifth palpable with 3 plus caput as a trial in theatre rather than a birth in the room, because caput and moulding routinely make a mid cavity head feel as though it is at the spines.

options.rationale: Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position, and applying them to a head in the transverse position would be a misapplication with a high risk of facial nerve injury and severe maternal trauma. The position alone excludes this instrument. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Augmentation with more time is reasonable for inadequate contractions with a well applied head making gradual progress, and this woman has already pushed for two hours with significant caput and moulding indicating obstruction. Adding another hour increases the risks of obstructed labour without addressing why the head has not descended. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally means that engagement is marginal and the station felt vaginally is being exaggerated by 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, which makes this a mid cavity birth with a transverse position and a genuine chance of failure. Conducting the attempt in theatre with the team assembled allows immediate progression to caesarean section if the instrument does not deliver, which is the arrangement that avoids a delayed second attempt with a deeply impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

A category one caesarean is for immediate threat to maternal or fetal life, and this cardiotocograph has normal variability with variable decelerations that recover within a minute, which does not meet that threshold. Committing straight to caesarean at full dilatation with the head at the spines also carries a real risk of a difficult impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Manual rotation followed by vacuum is a recognised technique for a transverse position and is appropriate when the head is well engaged with minimal caput and moulding. With two fifths palpable abdominally and marked caput, doing it in the room removes the immediate recourse to caesarean that this degree of uncertainty demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: This woman has two problems that one treatment addresses: troublesome vasomotor symptoms and osteopenia with a family history of hip fracture. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also prevents the rapid bone loss of the early postmenopausal years, which makes it the rational first choice. The timing hypothesis matters, since initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period carries a favourable balance of benefit and risk, whereas starting much later increases cardiovascular risk. A progestogen is mandatory alongside oestrogen in any woman with an intact uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. Bisphosphonates and denosumab are reserved for established osteoporosis rather than osteopenia in a symptomatic woman of this age.
key_points: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also preserves bone density.
The favourable window is initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period.
A progestogen is mandatory with systemic oestrogen in any woman who has an intact uterus.
Osteoporosis is defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or by a minimal trauma fracture.
Transdermal oestrogen carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than the oral route.
explanation.pearls: Treat osteopenia in a symptomatic woman within ten years of her last period with menopausal hormone therapy rather than a bisphosphonate, because it addresses the flushes and the bone loss together, and never prescribe systemic oestrogen without a progestogen when the uterus is intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

options.rationale: A bisphosphonate is first line for established osteoporosis defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or a minimal trauma fracture, neither of which she has. It also does nothing for the vasomotor symptoms that are her presenting problem and are the reason she has withdrawn from her activities. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

She is within ten years of her final menstrual period and under 60, the window in which the balance of benefit and risk for hormone therapy is most favourable, and it is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms while also preventing the accelerated bone loss of the early postmenopausal years. A progestogen must accompany the oestrogen because she has an intact uterus and unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

The transdermal route is a sound choice and carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than oral oestrogen, so the delivery method here is not the error. Giving oestrogen without a progestogen to a woman with an intact uterus is the error, because unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

Denosumab is a potent antiresorptive used in established osteoporosis, often where bisphosphonates are unsuitable, and it requires uninterrupted six monthly dosing because cessation causes rapid rebound bone loss with vertebral fractures. Committing a 53-year-old with osteopenia to that long term obligation is disproportionate. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

options.rationale: A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is a reasonable non hormonal option for flushes in women who cannot take or decline hormone therapy, and it is less effective than oestrogen and offers no skeletal benefit. She has no contraindication to hormone therapy, so accepting a weaker option for both of her problems is not justified. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: A symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue around the external os is columnar epithelium sitting on the outer cervix, which is a normal variant common in young women, in pregnancy and on oestrogen containing contraception. It bleeds on contact and is therefore an appealing explanation for postcoital bleeding, but it is present in many women without symptoms, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis. The important differential in a sexually active woman with a new partner is chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis, which commonly causes intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding with no discharge and no pain. Swabs are taken before the bleeding is attributed to the appearance, and treatment with partner notification follows a positive result. Colposcopy is reserved for a suspicious lesion, an abnormal screening result, or persistent bleeding once infection has been excluded and treated.
key_points: Columnar epithelium on the outer cervix is a normal variant that bleeds on contact.
It is present in many asymptomatic women, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis.
Chlamydial cervicitis commonly causes contact bleeding with no discharge or pain.
A negative human papillomavirus result makes significant cervical disease unlikely.
Persistent bleeding after infection is excluded and treated warrants colposcopy.
explanation.pearls: Never let a visible ectropion close the consultation in a woman under thirty with a new partner, because chlamydia causes the same contact bleeding, is usually silent otherwise, and the tubal damage it causes is what she presents with in ten years' time.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception

options.rationale: The appearance describes columnar epithelium extended onto the outer cervix, which is a normal finding in a young woman on oestrogen containing contraception and bleeds easily on contact. It is a common but unreliable explanation for the symptom, so infection must be excluded first, and chlamydial cervicitis in a woman with a new partner produces exactly this pattern of bleeding with no discharge or pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

Colposcopy is indicated for an irregular, ulcerated or friable mass, for persistent bleeding after infection has been excluded and treated, or for an abnormal screening result. A negative human papillomavirus test two years ago makes significant cervical disease very unlikely, and a symmetrical circumferential appearance is not the pattern of malignancy. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

The appearance genuinely is benign and does not itself require treatment, which is why this answer is tempting. Accepting it as the cause without excluding infection is how chlamydia is missed in exactly the group most likely to have it and most likely to suffer tubal damage from it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

Screening under the renewed program is five yearly after a negative result, so hers is not due and repeating it early does not change her management. A screening test is also not the right instrument for investigating a symptom, which is assessed on its own merits. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

Breakthrough bleeding in the first months of a new pill often settles, and changing the formulation is a reasonable step once other causes have been excluded. Reducing the oestrogen dose usually makes breakthrough bleeding worse rather than better, and it does nothing about an untreated infection. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception

explanation.summary: Rhesus D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitisation by clearing fetal red cells before the immune system responds to them, so the indication depends on whether enough fetal red cells could plausibly have entered the maternal circulation. Before 12 weeks the fetal red cell mass is tiny, and threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy is not considered a sensitising event in Australian guidance. Events before 12 weeks that do warrant the 250 IU dose are ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage involving instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. From 12 weeks the dose rises to 625 IU, and from 20 weeks a Kleihauer test is used to determine whether additional doses are needed. This woman continues on routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby types as rhesus D positive.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy does not require prophylaxis.
Sensitising events before 12 weeks warrant 250 IU, and from 12 weeks 625 IU.
Ectopic and molar pregnancy, termination and chorionic villus sampling are sensitising at any gestation.
Kleihauer testing guides additional dosing only from 20 weeks.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby is positive.
explanation.pearls: Anchor on 12 weeks and on whether the uterus was instrumented: bleeding alone before 12 weeks in a viable intrauterine pregnancy earns no immunoglobulin, but the same bleeding after a curette or a chorionic villus sample earns 250 IU within 72 hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Quantifying fetomaternal haemorrhage guides the dose after a sensitising event from 20 weeks, such as abdominal trauma or antepartum haemorrhage. Before 12 weeks the fetal red cell volume is below the detection threshold of the test, so a negative result carries no reassurance and no decision rests on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: That dose is the correct one for a sensitising event before 12 weeks, and such events include ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage with instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. Threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy at this gestation is specifically not on that list. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: The larger dose belongs to sensitising events from 12 weeks onward, so it is both the wrong indication and the wrong dose here. Repeating the antibody screen shortly after giving immunoglobulin is also unhelpful because passively acquired anti D cannot be distinguished from immune anti D on a routine screen. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Fetal blood group typing from maternal plasma is used in some settings to avoid unnecessary prophylaxis, but it is not part of routine Australian care and is not reliable this early in pregnancy. It would also delay a decision that does not need the information. (Source: Lifeblood: Anti D in pregnancy)

Prophylaxis is not recommended for threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks where the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable, because the fetomaternal haemorrhage at this gestation is too small to sensitise and the fetal red cell mass is minimal. She remains on the routine pathway, which is a dose at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, plus a dose after birth if the baby is rhesus D positive. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: The decision after a repaired anal sphincter injury turns on current function rather than on the fact of the previous tear. A woman with no incontinence, no urgency and normal endoanal ultrasound and manometry has adequate reserve, and the recurrence risk of about five to seven per cent does not outweigh the risks of planned abdominal delivery. Caesarean is recommended where symptoms persist or where testing shows a residual sphincter defect or low pressures, because a further vaginal birth can decompensate a sphincter that is only just coping. Routine episiotomy is not protective and midline episiotomy makes injury more likely, so intrapartum care focuses on controlled delivery of the head and perineal support. If an instrumental birth becomes necessary, vacuum carries a lower risk of sphincter injury than forceps.
key_points: Current continence and anorectal testing, not the previous tear itself, drive the recommendation.
Recurrence risk of sphincter injury is approximately five to seven per cent.
Persistent symptoms or an abnormal study shift the recommendation toward caesarean.
Routine episiotomy does not protect the sphincter and midline episiotomy increases injury.
Vacuum extraction carries a lower sphincter injury risk than forceps.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about leakage of flatus rather than of stool, because women rarely volunteer it and it is the symptom that most often identifies the compensated sphincter that will decompensate after a second vaginal birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: A woman who has no continence symptoms and normal anorectal testing after a repaired sphincter injury has a low risk of lasting deterioration and can be supported toward vaginal birth. The recurrence risk of a further sphincter injury is around five to seven per cent, which does not by itself justify abdominal surgery in an asymptomatic woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not prevent sphincter injury and midline episiotomy increases it, so it is performed for a clinical indication rather than as a prophylactic measure. Perineal protection during crowning and a warm compress have better evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Forceps carries a higher risk of sphincter injury than vacuum, so the operator can reasonably prefer vacuum if instrumental birth becomes necessary. Committing in advance to abdominal delivery rather than an assisted vaginal birth removes a safe option and increases the overall operative rate. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Repeat testing is worthwhile where symptoms have developed or where the earlier studies were equivocal, since the result would then change the recommendation. With normal studies and unchanged symptoms, repeating them delays the discussion without altering it. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Caesarean is recommended for women who remain symptomatic or who have abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, because a further vaginal birth can convert compensated function into frank incontinence. Applying it to every woman with a previous tear exposes a large number to operative risk for no measurable gain. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Chorionicity determined in the first trimester governs almost every subsequent decision in twin pregnancy, including the frequency of scans and the timing of birth. The lambda sign with two separate placental masses identifies a dichorionic pregnancy, in which each twin has its own placental circulation and the risks of twin to twin transfusion and sudden co twin demise do not apply. Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are therefore delivered at 37 to 38 weeks, while monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at 36 to 37 weeks and monoamniotic pregnancies considerably earlier. The rationale for not continuing past 38 weeks is the steep rise in stillbirth beyond that gestation rather than any problem in this pregnancy. Mode of birth is decided near term and vaginal birth remains appropriate when the first twin is cephalic, whatever the second twin is doing weeks beforehand.
key_points: The lambda sign with two placental masses indicates dichorionicity.
Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are delivered at 37 to 38 weeks.
Monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered earlier, at 36 to 37 weeks.
Stillbirth risk in twins rises steeply beyond 38 weeks.
The presentation of the second twin is determined at birth, not in the third trimester.
explanation.pearls: Go back to the 12 week images before you quote any timing, because chorionicity cannot be assigned reliably in the third trimester and getting it wrong shifts the planned birth by a full week in either direction.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: The lambda sign with two placental masses establishes a dichorionic pregnancy, which does not carry the vascular anastomoses responsible for the sudden losses seen in monochorionic twins, so birth is planned later than in those pregnancies. Beyond 38 weeks the stillbirth risk in dichorionic twins rises, and the presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks does not predict the presentation at birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: That earlier window applies to monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies, where shared placental circulation creates a risk of sudden intrauterine death that increases from the late third trimester. Applying it to a dichorionic pregnancy delivers a large number of babies early for a risk they do not carry. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Twin pregnancies have a higher stillbirth rate than singletons at every gestation and that rate climbs steeply beyond 38 weeks, which is why expectant management to term plus is not offered. Surveillance does not reliably predict the losses that occur in this window. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: The presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks changes frequently and is determined at the time of birth, not now, so it cannot drive the timing. Birth at 34 weeks in an uncomplicated pregnancy imposes substantial prematurity for no indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 108 g/L reflects the physiological dilution that is more pronounced in twins, and it is managed with iron studies and replacement rather than by delivery. It is not an indication for preterm birth in a woman with normal growth and Doppler studies. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fibroid treatment is chosen by matching the intervention to the dominant symptom and to the woman's reproductive intentions. Bulk symptoms such as pressure, frequency and abdominal distension respond to procedures that remove or shrink the fibroid, not to medical treatments aimed at bleeding. Because she intends to conceive next year, uterine artery embolisation is avoided, since its effects on ovarian reserve and placentation and its limited pregnancy outcome data make it unsuitable when fertility matters. Myomectomy preserves the uterus and relieves bulk symptoms, at the cost of a uterine scar that influences the mode of a future birth and a recurrence rate that rises over subsequent years. A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist has a place before surgery rather than instead of it.
key_points: Match the treatment to the dominant symptom: bulk symptoms need volume reduction.
Embolisation is avoided where future pregnancy is intended.
Myomectomy preserves the uterus but creates a scar that affects future birth planning.
A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist is a preoperative adjunct, not definitive treatment.
The intrauterine device treats bleeding but not pressure symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Ask what she wants fixed and when she wants to conceive before choosing anything, because the intrauterine device and embolisation both look attractive on paper and both are the wrong answer for a woman whose complaint is pressure and whose plan is pregnancy within the year.

options.rationale: Imaging is escalated where rapid growth after the menopause, unusual features or a suspicious ultrasound raise the possibility of a sarcoma, which is rare and cannot be excluded by imaging in any case. A typical fibroid on ultrasound in a woman of 34 does not warrant that pathway, though magnetic resonance imaging does have a role in mapping multiple fibroids before surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

The device reduces menstrual blood loss effectively and is a reasonable choice where heavy bleeding is the dominant problem and the cavity is normal. It does nothing for the pressure and urinary symptoms that bulk produces, and it is contraception she does not want. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms and avoids surgery, which makes it attractive for women who have completed their families. It is not recommended where pregnancy is planned because of concerns about ovarian reserve, placentation and miscarriage, and because outcome data in subsequent pregnancy remain limited. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

An agonist reduces fibroid volume and is used before surgery to correct anaemia or to make an operation more feasible, so it is an adjunct rather than a treatment. Fibroids regrow within months of stopping, and the induced hypo oestrogenic state causes bone loss and prevents conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

Surgical removal of the fibroid preserves the uterus and relieves pressure symptoms caused by bulk, which is what she has, and it remains the option with the best evidence when pregnancy is intended. She needs to know that a myomectomy entering the myometrium changes the plan for a future birth and that fibroids may recur. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

explanation.summary: Reduced fetal movement is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, and its importance lies in its association with growth restriction, placental insufficiency and subsequent stillbirth. Assessment therefore has two components that answer different questions: cardiotocography tells you how the fetus is now, and ultrasound for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler tells you whether the placenta is failing. A normal trace is common in a fetus that is nonetheless growth restricted, so it cannot be used alone to close the episode. This woman has two additional risk factors, a fundal height that has fallen behind and ongoing smoking, which make the scan more important rather than less. Provoking movements with cold drinks or position change has no evidence base and delays assessment.
key_points: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency.
Cardiotocography assesses current wellbeing and cannot detect growth restriction.
Ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler answers the placental question.
Symphysis fundal height falling behind or static is an indication for a growth scan.
Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth.
explanation.pearls: Plot the fundal height against the previous measurement before deciding anything, because a static or falling height alongside reduced movements is the combination most likely to precede stillbirth and it converts a reassuring trace into an indication for a scan the same day.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are given when preterm birth within seven days is anticipated, which is a decision that follows the assessment rather than preceding it. Continuous monitoring at 32 weeks without an abnormal finding commits her to admission without adding information. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth and they delay objective assessment in a woman who has already recognised a change and presented. Any manoeuvre intended to provoke movement is a substitute for the assessment rather than part of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.rationale: The biophysical profile includes cardiotocography as one of its components and adds ultrasound measures of tone, movement, breathing and liquor. It takes longer to organise and does not outperform the combination of an immediate trace with a growth and Doppler assessment in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.rationale: A normal cardiotocograph reflects fetal wellbeing at that moment and is reassuring in the short term, which is why it is done first. It does not detect growth restriction, so discharging on the trace alone misses the pathology that reduced movements most often signal, particularly when the fundal height has fallen. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.rationale: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency, so assessment has two parts: immediate assessment of fetal wellbeing by cardiotocography, and assessment of growth and placental function by ultrasound. Her fundal height has fallen behind and she smokes, both of which raise the pretest probability of a small or compromised fetus, so the scan is arranged rather than considered. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Bariatric procedures divide into restrictive operations such as sleeve gastrectomy, where oral absorption is largely preserved, and malabsorptive or combined procedures such as Roux en Y gastric bypass, where the shortened absorptive surface and accelerated transit make oral medicine absorption unreliable. After a bypass, oral contraceptives of any kind are avoided and a non oral method is recommended. Long-acting reversible methods suit this situation particularly well because pregnancy must be avoided through a prolonged period of rapid weight change, during which nutritional deficiencies and poor fetal growth are the concern. The early postoperative months also carry an elevated venous thromboembolism risk, which is a further reason to avoid an oestrogen containing method at this point. Women who conceive after weight loss surgery need close nutritional monitoring in pregnancy.
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures make absorption of any oral contraceptive unreliable.
Restrictive procedures such as sleeve gastrectomy largely preserve oral absorption.
Long-acting reversible methods bypass the gut and cover the whole period of weight change.
The early postoperative period carries elevated venous thromboembolism risk.
Pregnancy is generally avoided for twelve to eighteen months after surgery.
explanation.pearls: Ask which operation she had before choosing a method, because a sleeve gastrectomy leaves oral contraception perfectly viable while a bypass does not, and the two are routinely described by patients in the same words as weight loss surgery.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

options.rationale: Body weight does reduce the effectiveness of emergency contraception with levonorgestrel and of the contraceptive patch, so weight is a genuine consideration in method choice. Condoms have a typical use failure rate around thirteen per cent a year, which is not acceptable for a woman advised that pregnancy would be unsafe for eighteen months. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

options.rationale: It worked for her previously and her cardiovascular risk profile is otherwise unremarkable, which is why she is asking. The malabsorptive anatomy makes the oral route unreliable now, and the early postoperative period after a major abdominal operation is also the time of highest venous thromboembolism risk. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.rationale: A bypass procedure shortens the absorptive surface and speeds transit, so the absorption of any oral contraceptive becomes unreliable and failure rates rise. A device or an implant bypasses the gut entirely, gives several years of cover for a woman who must avoid pregnancy for eighteen months, and does not depend on the weight loss and dietary changes still under way. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.rationale: The ring does bypass the gut and is a legitimate non oral option from an absorption point of view, so the reasoning is half right. It still delivers systemic oestrogen soon after major abdominal surgery, and it requires correct use every month rather than providing years of cover. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.rationale: Moving from combined to progestogen only correctly removes the oestrogen and the associated thrombotic concern. It does not solve the problem, because absorption of the progestogen is affected by the same altered anatomy and this method already has the narrowest margin for a missed or delayed dose. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

explanation.summary: Valproate is the antiseizure medicine with the highest teratogenic risk, causing major congenital malformation in around one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment in a substantially larger proportion, with both effects rising with dose. Because organogenesis is largely complete before many women realise they are pregnant, the change must happen before conception, which means the referral is urgent and contraception continues until an alternative is established. Women taking any antiseizure medicine also need high dose folic acid of 5 mg daily started at least a month before conception, but folate does not mitigate the non neural tube effects of valproate. Abrupt cessation is dangerous because a generalised seizure carries its own risk of fetal hypoxia and maternal injury. Detailed morphology imaging remains part of antenatal care but detects rather than prevents harm.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformation in about one in ten exposed pregnancies.
Neurodevelopmental effects are dose related and are not prevented by folate.
Women on any antiseizure medicine take folic acid 5 mg daily from before conception.
Contraception continues until an alternative medicine is established.
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and fetal hypoxia.
explanation.pearls: Do not let the folate conversation substitute for the drug conversation: 5 mg of folic acid lowers neural tube defect risk but does nothing about the neurodevelopmental harm from valproate, which is the larger risk and the reason the neurologist needs to see her before she conceives.

options.rationale: Good seizure control is a genuine consideration and no change is made without a neurologist weighing it, which is why the referral is urgent rather than optional. Accepting a one in ten malformation risk without even attempting a switch is not a defensible position when effective alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus, and an uncontrolled generalised seizure in pregnancy threatens both the woman and the fetus through hypoxia and trauma. Any change is made gradually under specialist supervision with an alternative established first. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiepileptics)

Valproate carries roughly a one in ten risk of major congenital malformation and a much higher risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and both are dose related, so the priority is a planned switch to a safer agent before conception rather than after. Contraception continues during the switch because the transition takes months and an unplanned pregnancy in the interim exposes the fetus to the highest risk period. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Detailed imaging at 18 to 20 weeks does detect many structural malformations and will form part of her care in pregnancy. It is surveillance rather than prevention, and it cannot detect the neurodevelopmental harm that is the larger part of the risk from this drug. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

The higher folate dose is correct for a woman taking an antiseizure medicine and should be started at least one month before conception. It reduces neural tube defect risk but does not protect against the other malformations or the neurodevelopmental effects of valproate, so starting it while leaving the drug unchanged addresses only part of the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, so this couple qualifies and investigation should begin rather than be deferred. The first round of tests addresses the three commonest causes in parallel: male factor, ovulatory dysfunction and tubal disease. Semen analysis is the single highest yield test because male factor contributes in about half of couples and the result changes the entire subsequent pathway. A mid luteal progesterone taken seven days before the expected period confirms ovulation even when cycles look regular, and chlamydia testing identifies a treatable and frequently asymptomatic cause of tubal damage. Ovarian reserve testing, hysterosalpingography and laparoscopy each have a place but follow this first round rather than preceding it.
key_points: Infertility is defined at twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse.
Male factor contributes in about half of couples, so semen analysis comes first.
Mid luteal progesterone is taken seven days before the expected period.
Regular cycles do not guarantee ovulation and are confirmed biochemically.
Ovarian reserve testing predicts stimulation response rather than natural conception.
explanation.pearls: Investigate both partners at the same visit rather than working through her first, because half of these couples have a male factor and a delayed semen analysis is the commonest reason a workup takes a year instead of a month.

options.rationale: Laparoscopy directly visualises endometriosis and adhesions and is the right investigation where there is pelvic pain, painful intercourse or a suspicious history. As a first line test in a woman with no symptoms and no risk factors it exposes her to a general anaesthetic ahead of the non-invasive assessments. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

A male factor contributes in around half of couples and semen analysis is inexpensive, non-invasive and abnormal often enough that it belongs in the first round for every couple. A mid luteal progesterone confirms that her regular cycles are genuinely ovulatory, and testing for chlamydia matters because previous asymptomatic infection is a common and treatable cause of tubal damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

Advice about the fertile window is useful for couples who are mistiming intercourse, and reviewing frequency of intercourse is part of the history. Fourteen months of regular unprotected intercourse already meets the definition of infertility, so investigation is indicated now rather than after a further delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

Ovarian reserve testing predicts the response to ovarian stimulation and is therefore useful once assisted reproduction is being planned. It is a poor predictor of natural conception in a woman of 29 with regular cycles and does not explain why this couple has not conceived. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

Tubal patency assessment is an important part of the workup and follows once ovulation and semen quality are known, since an abnormal semen analysis changes the whole pathway. Referring for treatment before any test has been done skips the step that determines which treatment is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

explanation.summary: Aura is defined by fully reversible focal neurological symptoms that develop over several minutes and precede or accompany the headache, most often visual and most often described as zigzag lines or a shimmering scotoma. Its importance in contraceptive prescribing is that migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so oestrogen containing methods are unacceptable at any age and any dose. The restriction applies to the pill, the patch and the ring equally, because it follows the systemic oestrogen rather than the route. Progestogen only methods and the copper intrauterine device carry no such association and are all available to her. Migraine without aura is treated differently and combined contraception can usually be used with review.
key_points: Aura consists of fully reversible focal symptoms developing over minutes before the headache.
Migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk.
Combined hormonal contraception is unacceptable with aura at any oestrogen dose.
The restriction applies equally to the pill, the patch and the ring.
Progestogen only methods and the copper device carry no arterial risk restriction.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the visual symptom comes before the headache and goes away completely, because photophobia and blurred vision during a migraine are not aura, while twenty minutes of zigzag lines beforehand rules out every oestrogen containing method she might ask for.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.rationale: Focal neurological symptoms preceding a headache and resolving before it starts identify migraine with aura, which raises ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so it is unacceptable regardless of age or other risk factors. Progestogen only methods carry no such stroke association and are unrestricted in these women, which leaves her the full range of long acting and oral options. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.rationale: Lowering the oestrogen dose reduces venous thromboembolism risk but does not remove the arterial risk that matters here, and no dose of oestrogen is considered acceptable alongside aura. Monitoring cannot detect an impending stroke. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.rationale: Continuous regimens genuinely reduce the oestrogen withdrawal headaches that occur in the hormone free interval, which is useful for migraine without aura. That strategy does not apply to a woman who should not be taking oestrogen at all, and her headaches currently occur without any hormonal cycling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Migraine)

The copper device is a perfectly reasonable option for her and carries no hormonal risk at all. Restricting her to it alone misstates the evidence, because it is oestrogen rather than hormonal contraception in general that is contraindicated, and it may worsen the heavy bleeding some women experience. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.rationale: Route of administration changes hepatic exposure and some metabolic effects, but the systemic oestrogen and the arterial risk remain, so the ring and the patch are restricted in exactly the same way as the pill. The contraindication follows the hormone rather than the delivery method. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

explanation.summary: Cyclical pelvic pain beginning before the period, continuing through it and accompanied by deep pain during intercourse is a typical history for endometriosis, and a normal ultrasound does not argue against it because superficial peritoneal disease cannot be seen on any imaging. Australian guidance has moved away from requiring laparoscopic confirmation before treatment, so medical management is started on the clinical picture and the diagnosis is supported by the response. Continuous combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation and menstruation and addresses the cyclical mechanism, and it suits a woman who also needs contraception. Anti inflammatories work best taken regularly from before the pain begins rather than as rescue once it is established. Surgery, agonist therapy and multidisciplinary pain management all remain available if this approach fails or if fertility becomes the presenting issue.
key_points: A normal pelvic ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal disease.
Treatment is started on the clinical picture without requiring laparoscopic confirmation.
Continuous hormonal suppression targets the cyclical mechanism of the pain.
Anti inflammatories are most effective taken regularly from before the pain starts.
Agonist therapy with add back is reserved for failure of first line hormonal treatment.
explanation.pearls: Tell her to start the anti inflammatory the day before her period is due rather than when the pain arrives, because prostaglandin release has already happened by the time she reaches for the tablet and that single change in timing often doubles the benefit she gets from it.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Agonist treatment is effective and is used when first line hormonal treatment has failed or is not tolerated, with add back therapy to limit bone loss and vasomotor symptoms. Starting with it in a woman who has not yet tried simpler options exposes her to those adverse effects unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Pelvic floor physiotherapy and pain psychology are genuinely valuable in persistent pelvic pain and belong in the longer term plan, particularly where central sensitisation has developed. Offering them instead of hormonal suppression at the first visit withholds the treatment that addresses the cyclical mechanism driving her pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endometriosis)

Laparoscopy establishes the diagnosis histologically and treats lesions at the same time, and it is appropriate where medical treatment has failed, where fertility is an immediate concern or where deep disease is suspected. Requiring it before any treatment delays relief by months and exposes a young woman to surgery she may never need. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Imaging is valuable for mapping deep infiltrating disease and endometrioma before surgery, and transvaginal ultrasound by an experienced operator detects much of this. Superficial peritoneal disease is invisible on all imaging, so a normal scan neither excludes the condition nor changes the first line medical plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation and menstruation treats the cyclical pain of this condition and is offered on the clinical picture without waiting for surgical confirmation, since laparoscopy is no longer required to begin treatment. Taking the anti inflammatory regularly from before the pain begins works far better than taking it once the pain is established, and she also gains the contraception she currently lacks. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

explanation.summary: Screening of cell free DNA in maternal plasma analyses fragments derived from the placenta, which usually but not always reflect the fetal karyotype. It performs very well for trisomy 21 and reasonably for trisomies 18 and 13, but it returns a probability rather than a diagnosis, and the positive predictive value falls considerably for rarer conditions and in younger women. Confined placental mosaicism, a vanishing twin, maternal mosaicism and maternal malignancy all generate results that do not reflect the fetus, which is why chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis is required before any irreversible decision. The test does not assess fetal structure, so the first trimester and morphology ultrasounds remain part of care. It is not rebated by Medicare in Australia and all prenatal screening is voluntary.
key_points: The test analyses placental DNA and returns a probability, not a diagnosis.
A high chance result requires chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis to confirm.
Confined placental mosaicism and a vanishing twin are recognised causes of discordant results.
The test does not assess fetal structure and does not replace ultrasound.
It is not rebated by Medicare and all prenatal screening is voluntary.
explanation.pearls: Say the words screening test and diagnostic test explicitly in the consultation and write them down, because women commonly leave believing they have had the baby's chromosomes checked, and that misunderstanding is what drives decisions made on an unconfirmed high chance result.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions
Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Advancing maternal age does raise the chance of trisomy and makes the offer of screening more relevant, so the discussion is appropriate. All prenatal screening is voluntary and declining it is a legitimate choice that does not affect the rest of her care. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.rationale: Detection is very high for trisomy 21 and good for trisomies 18 and 13, which is why a low chance result is genuinely reassuring for those conditions. It says nothing about the many single gene disorders, microdeletions and structural anomalies that the test does not examine. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.rationale: Screening for chromosomal conditions from maternal plasma does not assess fetal structure, and ultrasound remains necessary to detect structural anomalies, to confirm dating and viability and to assess the placenta. The first trimester scan also identifies findings such as a markedly increased nuchal translucency that carry their own implications. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: The test analyses placental DNA circulating in maternal plasma and returns a probability rather than a diagnosis, so a high chance result must be confirmed by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis before any irreversible decision is made. Confined placental mosaicism, a vanishing twin and maternal chromosomal variation all produce results that do not reflect the fetal karyotype. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.rationale: Cost matters to families and should be discussed, because this test is paid for privately in Australia and the amount is not trivial. There is no age based rebate, and getting this wrong sends women away expecting a refund that will not come. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed by pruritus without a primary rash together with raised bile acids, after excluding other liver disease. Its significance is almost entirely fetal, and the pivotal insight from large cohort data is that risk is not uniform across the diagnosis but is concentrated in women with severe biochemical disease. Peak bile acid concentration stratifies that risk, with levels below 40 micromol/L carrying little excess stillbirth risk and levels of 100 micromol/L or above carrying a markedly elevated risk that justifies planned late preterm birth. Because the stillbirth is typically sudden rather than preceded by growth restriction or abnormal Dopplers, antenatal surveillance offers false reassurance and timing of birth is the only intervention shown to matter.
key_points: Diagnosis requires pruritus with raised bile acids and exclusion of other liver disease
Peak bile acid concentration stratifies stillbirth risk within the diagnosis
Levels of 100 micromol/L or above justify planned birth at 35 to 36 weeks
Cardiotocography and Doppler do not predict the sudden stillbirth
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but not stillbirth risk
explanation.pearls: The 100 micromol/L bile acid threshold is the single number that changes management in cholestasis of pregnancy, moving planned birth from around 38 weeks to 35 to 36 weeks with corticosteroid cover.

options.rationale: Stillbirth risk rises steeply once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L, and this threshold defines the group in whom earlier planned birth is justified. Corticosteroids are given because birth at this gestation carries neonatal respiratory risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

This timing suits women whose bile acids remain below 40 micromol/L, where the excess stillbirth risk is not clearly increased. It underestimates the risk carried by a level above 100 micromol/L. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden stillbirth associated with this condition, so surveillance cannot substitute for earlier birth. The timing also does not reflect the severity band she now occupies. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but has not been shown to reduce stillbirth, so it cannot justify expectant management to term. Treating the symptom does not address the risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Birth at 33 weeks would expose the baby to substantial prematurity risk that outweighs the stillbirth risk at this gestation. Immediate birth is reserved for other deteriorating features such as jaundice with coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin routinely in the third trimester, after birth of a rhesus positive baby, and after potentially sensitising events. The distinction that causes most difficulty in early pregnancy is between a threatened miscarriage with a viable pregnancy and a genuine sensitising event such as miscarriage with instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy, termination, or chorionic villus sampling. Before 12 weeks the feto-maternal transfusion volume in uncomplicated threatened miscarriage is too small to sensitise, so anti-D is not indicated. Dose also varies by gestation, with 250 IU covering first trimester events and 625 IU used after 12 weeks alongside a Kleihauer test to detect a larger bleed requiring additional doses.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks with a viable pregnancy does not need anti-D
Instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy and termination are sensitising at any gestation
First trimester sensitising events are covered by a 250 IU dose
After 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU with a Kleihauer test to quantify the bleed
Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given irrespective of earlier events
explanation.pearls: Anti-D must be given within 72 hours of a sensitising event to be reliably effective, though it is still worth giving up to ten days later if the window has been missed.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin
National Blood Authority Australia: Anti-D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Giving anti-D for a threatened miscarriage at this gestation exposes her to a blood product without evidence of benefit. The 250 IU dose is correct for first trimester sensitising events, but this is not one. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Anti-D is not required for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks where the pregnancy remains viable and there has been no instrumentation, because the feto-maternal transfusion volume is negligible. Routine prophylaxis will still be given in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: The larger dose and quantification of feto-maternal haemorrhage apply to sensitising events after 12 weeks, not to first trimester bleeding. Both the dose and the test are mismatched to the gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Fetal genotyping from maternal blood is not part of routine Australian practice and would not alter management at this gestation. The decision here rests on whether a sensitising event has occurred. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given to all rhesus negative women regardless of first trimester events. Omitting it would leave her unprotected against silent sensitisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is confirmed on sterile speculum examination rather than by digital examination, which should be avoided because it introduces infection and shortens latency. Management balances the risk of ascending infection against the risks of prematurity, and while both surveillance and the threshold for birth shift with gestation, expectant management is preferred well before term. Latency antibiotics are given to prolong the interval to birth, with a macrolide chosen because amoxicillin with clavulanic acid increases neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Antenatal corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity, and magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks. Signs of chorioamnionitis, including maternal fever, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, maternal tachycardia or fetal tachycardia, convert the plan to immediate birth with intravenous antibiotics.
key_points: Diagnosis is by sterile speculum examination, avoiding digital examination
Latency antibiotics use a macrolide, not amoxicillin with clavulanate
Tocolysis is not recommended after membranes rupture
Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is expected before 30 weeks
Chorioamnionitis converts management from expectant to immediate birth
explanation.pearls: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is specifically avoided as the latency antibiotic in ruptured preterm membranes because of the increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis demonstrated in the ORACLE trial.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: This combination is specifically avoided in this setting because it is associated with an increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. The principle of latency antibiotics is right but the agent is wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Latency antibiotics prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity, and corticosteroids reduce respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis at this gestation. With no evidence of infection or fetal compromise, expectant management allows further maturation. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended once membranes have ruptured because it does not improve outcomes and may prolong exposure to intrauterine infection. She is not contracting in any case. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Immediate birth at 30 weeks exchanges a small infection risk for substantial prematurity, and expectant management is preferred while surveillance remains reassuring. Planned birth becomes appropriate closer to 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Amnioinfusion has no established role in managing ruptured membranes remote from term and introduces an additional intrauterine procedure. The fluid volume here is in any case at the lower limit of normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormally adherent or invasive placentation, and its incidence has risen in step with caesarean section rates. The combination that should prompt suspicion is an anterior low lying placenta in a woman with previous uterine surgery, since the placenta implants over a scarred, poorly decidualised segment. Sonographic markers include loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae, bladder wall interface irregularity and increased subplacental vascularity on Doppler. The single intervention that most reduces maternal morbidity is planned birth at around 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with a multidisciplinary team, massive transfusion capability and interventional radiology, since unanticipated accreta discovered at an emergency caesarean carries far higher rates of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission and death.
key_points: Anterior low placenta plus previous caesarean is the classic risk combination
Loss of the clear zone and vascular lacunae suggest invasion rather than praevia
Invasion features do not resolve with advancing gestation
Planned birth in a tertiary centre is the main determinant of maternal outcome
Unanticipated accreta at emergency caesarean carries the worst outcomes
explanation.pearls: A woman with an anterior placenta praevia and two previous caesareans has a risk of placenta accreta spectrum of roughly forty per cent, which is why the finding prompts tertiary referral rather than a repeat scan.

options.rationale: Loss of the clear zone with lacunae in an anterior placenta overlying a previous scar indicates abnormal placental invasion rather than simple praevia. Outcomes are substantially better when birth occurs in a centre with interventional radiology, blood bank and gynaecological oncology or urology support available. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Rescanning at 32 weeks with a local caesarean is the pathway for uncomplicated placenta praevia, where migration is common and local birth is reasonable. The invasion features here mean the problem is not the position of the placenta but its attachment. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia)

Reassurance based on migration ignores the sonographic features of invasion, which do not resolve and carry a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. It also defers referral past the point where planning is useful. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Prolonged admission does not address the need for a surgical team and resources capable of managing massive haemorrhage. Where the birth happens matters more than how long she is observed beforehand. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Imaging may refine the assessment but committing to hysterectomy at this gestation and at a unit without the necessary support reverses the priorities. The location of birth is the decision that changes outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean section is offered to suitable women in Australian practice, with uterine scar rupture the principal risk at roughly one in two hundred labours. Because rupture is uncommon, its recognition depends on assembling several individually unremarkable findings rather than on any single sign. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest feature, and it is often accompanied by constant abdominal pain between contractions, cessation or weakening of previously effective contractions, loss of station of the presenting part, vaginal bleeding, haematuria, and maternal tachycardia with hypotension. Scar pain alone is a poor discriminator, particularly with an epidural in place. Management is immediate laparotomy, and the interval from diagnosis to delivery is the strongest determinant of neonatal outcome, so no investigation should precede transfer to theatre.
key_points: Scar rupture complicates roughly one in two hundred labours after caesarean
An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign
Loss of station and fading contractions indicate loss of uterine integrity
Epidural analgesia masks scar pain and reduces its diagnostic value
Time from diagnosis to delivery determines neonatal outcome
explanation.pearls: Weakening contractions in a woman labouring with a uterine scar is an ominous rather than a reassuring change, and augmenting with oxytocin at that moment can extend an existing rupture.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is used for fetal distress from uterine hyperstimulation, where contractions are excessive rather than fading. It would delay definitive treatment of a mechanical catastrophe. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Improving trace quality addresses monitoring rather than the underlying event, and the presenting part is now too high to attach an electrode safely. The clinical picture already establishes urgency. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Intrauterine resuscitation measures are appropriate for a deceleration from cord compression or hypotension, neither of which explains the loss of station and constant pain. They should not delay transfer to theatre here. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Augmenting a uterus that may have ruptured risks extending the defect and causing catastrophic haemorrhage. Weakening contractions here reflect loss of uterine integrity rather than inadequate labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Loss of station with constant pain, a deteriorating fetal heart rate and altered contractions in a scarred uterus indicates scar rupture, and both mother and baby are salvaged only by immediate operative delivery. Delay to confirm the diagnosis worsens outcomes for both. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is rare but is one of the few obstetric emergencies where the correct first move is counterintuitive and the wrong one makes the situation irretrievable. It is suspected when shock is out of proportion to measured blood loss, the fundus cannot be palpated abdominally, and a mass is found in the vagina or at the introitus, usually after excessive cord traction with a fundal placenta. The profound bradycardia reflects vagal stimulation from traction on the infundibulopelvic ligaments and distinguishes it from hypovolaemic shock, in which tachycardia is expected. Immediate manual replacement by pushing the fundus back through the cervix gives the best chance of success, and uterotonics are deliberately withheld until the uterus is restored, after which they are given to maintain tone. If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic reduction or surgical approaches are used, with tocolysis to relax the constriction ring.
key_points: Shock disproportionate to blood loss with an impalpable fundus suggests inversion
Bradycardia rather than tachycardia reflects the vagal mechanism
Excessive cord traction with a fundal placenta is the usual precipitant
Uterotonics are withheld until the fundus has been replaced
Hydrostatic or surgical reduction follows failed manual replacement
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia in a shocked woman immediately after birth should prompt palpation for the fundus, because vagally mediated bradycardia with an impalpable fundus is uterine inversion until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: Immediate replacement is the priority because the constriction ring tightens with time and makes later reduction progressively harder. Uterotonics are withheld until the fundus is replaced because they contract the ring and lock the inversion in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

A uterotonic given before reduction tightens the cervical ring around the inverted fundus and can make manual replacement impossible. The sequence is what matters, not the drug itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

Tamponade treats atonic bleeding from a correctly positioned uterus and cannot be deployed into an inverted one. The shock here is largely neurogenic rather than from measured loss. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Compression is a holding measure for atony and does nothing to correct the anatomical abnormality that is causing the collapse. Fluids alone will not reverse the vagal response. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Surgical reduction is reserved for failure of manual replacement, and the delay involved in transfer allows the ring to tighten further. Manual replacement should be attempted first at the bedside. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum hypopituitarism caused by infarction of a pituitary gland that has enlarged during pregnancy and is vulnerable to a period of hypotension from obstetric haemorrhage. Its presentation is easily missed because the early symptoms of fatigue, dizziness and poor appetite are ubiquitous after a difficult birth, and the most specific early clue, failure of lactation, is frequently attributed to stress or poor technique. The biochemical signature is a combination of deficiencies rather than a single abnormality, typically hyponatraemia with hypoglycaemia from cortisol deficiency and a low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal or low thyroid stimulating hormone, which distinguishes central from primary hypothyroidism. Later features include amenorrhoea and loss of secondary sexual hair. Replacement is lifelong and the order of starting matters critically.
key_points: Obstetric haemorrhage with hypotension is the precipitating event
Failure of lactation is the earliest specific clue and is easily dismissed
Low free thyroxine with a normal or low thyroid stimulating hormone indicates central failure
Hydrocortisone is always started before thyroxine replacement
Hyponatraemia with hypoglycaemia reflects cortisol rather than thyroid deficiency
explanation.pearls: A normal thyroid stimulating hormone alongside a low free thyroxine is the finding that reveals pituitary rather than thyroid failure, and in this setting it means hydrocortisone must precede the first thyroxine dose.

options.rationale: Giving thyroxine to a cortisol deficient patient accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate a crisis, which is why the order of replacement is fixed. The hormone choice is right but the sequence is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

This is the approach to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, which does not cause postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia or failure of lactation. Restricting fluid here would worsen her volume depletion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Pituitary failure after obstetric haemorrhage produces combined cortisol and thyroid deficiency, and cortisol must be replaced first because thyroxine raises metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The low sodium with hypoglycaemia and postural hypotension reflects the cortisol deficit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Treating the lactation failure in isolation misses the systemic endocrine cause and leaves the dangerous cortisol deficiency untreated. Her iron status is already satisfactory. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or severe neurological symptoms from hyponatraemia, and she has neither. Her sodium will correct as the hormone deficiency is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: A mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is one of the highest risk maternal cardiac situations, because pregnancy is prothrombotic while the anticoagulant that best protects the valve is the one that harms the fetus. Warfarin gives the lowest rate of valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta, causing a dose related embryopathy when taken between six and twelve weeks and increasing fetal intracranial haemorrhage near term. Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta but requires weight adjusted twice daily dosing with regular anti-Xa monitoring, and inadequate dosing has been associated with fatal valve thrombosis. Strategies therefore include continuing warfarin throughout with a switch near term, or substituting heparin during the embryopathy window, with the decision influenced by whether the daily warfarin dose exceeds 5 mg. All of this requires pre-pregnancy counselling by a multidisciplinary team, and the single most dangerous action is an unplanned unilateral cessation of anticoagulation.
key_points: Pregnancy is prothrombotic and mechanical valves need uninterrupted anticoagulation
Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose related and concentrated between six and twelve weeks
Low molecular weight heparin needs weight adjusted dosing with anti-Xa monitoring
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves
Pre-pregnancy multidisciplinary counselling precedes any change in therapy
explanation.pearls: A warfarin maintenance dose of 5 mg daily or less carries a substantially lower embryopathy risk, which is why the actual daily dose is the number that shapes the first trimester anticoagulation plan.

options.rationale: Every anticoagulation strategy in this setting trades maternal valve thrombosis against fetal risk, and the choice depends on her warfarin dose, valve position and preference, so it needs specialist discussion before conception. Stopping anticoagulation without a bridging plan carries a high risk of valve thrombosis, which is the leading cause of maternal death in this group. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

An unbridged gap in anticoagulation risks prosthetic valve thrombosis, which carries high maternal mortality and often occurs before she would be reviewed. Any change must be planned with an alternative agent already in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves because trials showed increased thromboembolism and bleeding compared with warfarin. They are also not recommended in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Antiplatelet therapy does not prevent thrombosis on a mechanical valve, which requires anticoagulation. Substituting it would leave the prosthesis effectively unprotected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Warfarin crosses the placenta and carries a dose related embryopathy risk in the first trimester as well as fetal bleeding risk later, so it cannot be presented as free of fetal consequence. Blanket reassurance would remove her ability to make an informed choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by first establishing whether secondary sexual characteristics have developed, because that single observation splits the differential efficiently. Absent breast development indicates absent oestrogen exposure, and gonadotrophins then separate a failing gonad, which drives them up, from a failing hypothalamus or pituitary, which leaves them low. Turner syndrome is the commonest chromosomal cause of gonadal failure and should be suspected whenever short stature accompanies absent breast development, with supportive features including a broad chest, widely spaced nipples, a webbed neck, a low hairline, lymphoedema and cubitus valgus. Because the pubic and axillary hair are driven by adrenal androgens rather than by the ovary, they develop normally and their presence is reassuring only about the adrenal axis. Diagnosis matters well beyond fertility, since it prompts screening for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic root dilatation, renal anomalies, hypothyroidism and coeliac disease, and growth hormone can improve final height if started early enough.
key_points: Presence or absence of breast development is the first branch point
Raised gonadotrophins localise the problem to the gonad rather than the pituitary
Pubic hair is adrenal driven and can be normal despite ovarian failure
Short stature with absent breast development should prompt a karyotype
Diagnosis triggers cardiac, aortic, renal and thyroid surveillance
explanation.pearls: Aortic root dilatation with a risk of dissection is the complication of Turner syndrome that persists into adult life and into pregnancy, so the karyotype result changes cardiac surveillance rather than only explaining the amenorrhoea.

options.rationale: Giving oestrogen before the diagnosis is established removes the diagnostic value of the gonadotrophins and may close the epiphyses prematurely in a girl who could benefit from growth treatment. Sequencing matters before any hormone is given. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
