Pituitary imaging is directed at hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, suggested by headache, visual field loss or impaired smell, none of which is present. Her short stature and dysmorphic features point elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

Constitutional delay usually follows a family pattern and does not produce height this far below the mid-parental target with dysmorphic features. Waiting a further year would forfeit the window for growth intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

Short stature with absent breast development but normal adrenal driven pubic hair indicates gonadal failure, and raised gonadotrophins would confirm the ovary rather than the pituitary as the site. A karyotype is essential because a chromosomal cause carries cardiac, renal and aortic implications that change lifelong care. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

Androgen excess would be suggested by hirsutism, acne and virilisation with normal or advanced growth, and she has none of these. Her pubic hair is normal rather than excessive. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is conventionally defined as three or more consecutive pregnancy losses, though investigation is often begun after two in older women or where there is another concern. The great majority of sporadic first trimester losses are caused by fetal chromosomal abnormality, and even after three losses no cause is identified in around half of couples, which is important to convey because the prognosis for a subsequent live birth remains good. The investigations that are worth doing are those attached to an intervention or to meaningful counselling: antiphospholipid antibodies, because aspirin with low molecular weight heparin improves live birth rates in confirmed cases, imaging of the uterine cavity for structural anomalies, and thyroid function. Antiphospholipid testing requires two positive results at least twelve weeks apart to confirm the diagnosis. A wide range of other tests, including inherited thrombophilia panels and immune assays, are frequently marketed to distressed couples but are not supported and can lead to unproven and potentially harmful treatment.
key_points: Three consecutive losses is the conventional threshold for investigation
No cause is found in around half of couples and the prognosis remains good
Antiphospholipid syndrome is the cause with the clearest effective treatment
Confirmation requires two positive antibody results twelve weeks apart
Inherited thrombophilia and immune panels are not part of standard assessment
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be positive on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart before the diagnosis is made, because transient positivity after an acute event is common and would otherwise commit a woman to unnecessary anticoagulation.

options.rationale: Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended for recurrent first trimester loss because the association is weak and anticoagulation has not improved outcomes. The acquired antibody syndrome is a different matter. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Peripheral natural killer cell testing has no established relationship with uterine immune function and is offered mainly outside the evidence base. Acting on the result exposes women to unproven immunotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one cause of recurrent loss with a treatment that clearly improves live birth rates, and structural uterine anomalies are the other reliably identifiable factor. Parental karyotyping is offered selectively because a balanced translocation in a parent changes counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not part of standard recurrent miscarriage assessment and no intervention based on it has been shown to improve live birth. It would not alter management here. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Three consecutive losses meets the threshold at which investigation is offered, and a treatable cause would otherwise be missed. Reassurance about prognosis is appropriate but accompanies rather than replaces assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate has two entirely separate obstetric indications that share a drug and nothing else. As eclampsia prophylaxis it is given for severe pre-eclampsia to prevent seizures, while as a neuroprotective agent it is given to women in very preterm labour to reduce cerebral palsy in the child, with roughly one case of cerebral palsy avoided for every 60 or so women treated. The Australian guideline applies the neuroprotective indication before 30 weeks of gestation when birth is planned or anticipated within 24 hours, regardless of the cause of the preterm birth, the plurality of the pregnancy or the mode of birth. Administration requires monitoring of respiratory rate, reflexes and urine output, since toxicity manifests as loss of deep tendon reflexes before respiratory depression, and calcium gluconate should be available.
key_points: Neuroprotection and eclampsia prophylaxis are separate indications for the same drug
The neuroprotective indication applies before 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours
Blood pressure and proteinuria are irrelevant to the neuroprotective decision
Benefit requires antenatal administration so the fetus is exposed before birth
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output during the infusion
explanation.pearls: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity and precedes respiratory depression, so hourly reflex checks matter more than routine serum magnesium levels in a woman with normal renal function.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Normal blood pressure excludes the seizure prophylaxis indication but is irrelevant to the neuroprotective one, which depends only on gestation and the imminence of birth. Conflating the two indications is the commonest reason this treatment is missed. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: This restricts magnesium to eclampsia prophylaxis, which is a separate indication with a different rationale and dosing intent. The neuroprotective benefit is lost entirely if treatment waits for hypertensive features that may never appear. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not effective once the cervix is 5 cm with ruptured membranes, and its purpose is to buy time for steroids and transfer rather than to replace neuroprotection. Omitting magnesium forfeits a benefit that applies whether or not birth is delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

Magnesium sulfate given to women before 30 weeks when birth is planned or expected within 24 hours reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in the surviving child, and this benefit is independent of blood pressure. At 28 weeks and 3 days with a cervix of 5 cm she meets both the gestational and the timing criteria. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: The neuroprotective effect depends on magnesium crossing the placenta and being present in the fetal circulation during labour and birth, so postnatal administration to the neonate does not reproduce it. Neonatal magnesium is used for different indications entirely. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses arise when the duct at the posterior introitus obstructs, and the central management principle is that the problem is the blocked duct rather than the fluid inside it. Procedures that simply evacuate the contents, including needle aspiration and simple incision and drainage, allow the opening to seal and carry recurrence rates that rise with each episode. Definitive management creates a permanent epithelialised channel, achieved either by a Word catheter left in for two to four weeks or by marsupialisation, where the cyst wall is sutured to the vulval skin. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features or sexually transmitted infection, and a new solid or persistent mass in a woman over 40 warrants biopsy because vulval gland carcinoma, although rare, presents this way.
key_points: The pathology is duct obstruction, so drainage alone predictably recurs
A Word catheter or marsupialisation creates a lasting epithelialised tract
The catheter stays in for two to four weeks to allow epithelialisation
Antibiotics are reserved for cellulitis or systemic involvement
A persistent mass over the age of 40 requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A new or persistent Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 should be biopsied rather than simply drained, because adenocarcinoma of the gland presents as an apparently benign recurrent swelling.

options.rationale: Simple incision relieves pain but the edges seal within days, which reforms a closed cavity and explains why this has now happened twice. It is the intervention that has already failed her. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

An established fluctuant abscess needs drainage, and antibiotics alone will not resolve a walled off collection of this size. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic features, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Excision is reserved for repeated failure of drainage procedures because it carries significant bleeding risk, scarring and dyspareunia. It is too morbid a step while a simpler definitive option has not yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

Aspiration decompresses the cavity temporarily but leaves no drainage tract at all, so the recurrence rate is higher than with simple incision. It offers no advantage over the approach that has already failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

The balloon tipped catheter is left in place for several weeks so the tract epithelialises, creating a lasting drainage channel and reducing recurrence far below that of simple incision. It is performed under local anaesthetic and preserves gland function and lubrication. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is distinguished from ordinary nausea and vomiting of pregnancy by weight loss exceeding about five per cent of body weight, dehydration, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance. Management combines rehydration with normal saline, potassium replacement guided by levels, and a stepwise antiemetic ladder, while thyroid function is checked because a transient biochemical hyperthyroidism driven by human chorionic gonadotrophin is common and rarely needs treatment. The critical prescribing point is thiamine: stores last only a few weeks, and administering glucose to a depleted woman consumes the last of the cofactor needed for carbohydrate metabolism, which can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Wernicke encephalopathy in pregnancy carries a high rate of lasting cognitive deficit and fetal loss, and is entirely preventable by giving thiamine first.
key_points: Hyperemesis requires weight loss, dehydration and ketosis, not just vomiting
Rehydrate with normal saline rather than dextrose containing fluid
Parenteral thiamine precedes any glucose load after prolonged vomiting
Transient hCG driven biochemical hyperthyroidism rarely needs treatment
Parenteral nutrition is a last resort because of line related complications
explanation.pearls: Any woman vomiting in pregnancy for more than three weeks should receive parenteral thiamine before intravenous glucose, because Wernicke encephalopathy can be precipitated by a single litre of dextrose.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: This is the plan as written and carries the specific hazard of precipitating an acute thiamine deficient encephalopathy in a woman whose stores are depleted after four weeks without intake. Dextrose is also a poor resuscitation fluid because it distributes across total body water. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Choosing saline over dextrose is correct, but deferring thiamine to the oral route in a woman who cannot keep fluids down means she effectively receives none. Replacement must be parenteral until absorption is reliable. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Four weeks of vomiting exhausts thiamine stores, and a glucose load consumes the remaining thiamine as a cofactor, which can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours. Parenteral thiamine is therefore given first, and rehydration then proceeds with normal saline and added potassium. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Her potassium does need replacing, but it can be added to the rehydration fluid rather than sequenced ahead of everything else, and withholding thiamine leaves the encephalopathy risk unaddressed. Potassium at this level is not immediately life threatening. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a last resort in hyperemesis because of line sepsis and thrombosis risk, and it is considered only after antiemetics, rehydration and enteral options have failed. Introducing a large glucose load without thiamine would compound the same hazard. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

explanation.summary: Recurrent urinary tract infection is defined as two episodes in six months or three in a year, and in postmenopausal women with a structurally normal tract the dominant mechanism is the genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Falling oestrogen thins the urogenital epithelium, raises vaginal pH and depletes lactobacilli, which permits colonisation by bowel uropathogens, so restoring local oestrogen addresses the cause rather than suppressing the consequence. Vaginal oestrogen has good trial evidence for reducing recurrence and is preferred to continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, which works only while taken and selects for resistance. Investigation for a structural cause is reserved for red flags such as persistent haematuria, infection with urea splitting organisms, a significant post-void residual or failure to respond to appropriate therapy.
key_points: Recurrent infection means two episodes in six months or three in twelve
Oestrogen deficiency raises vaginal pH and depletes protective lactobacilli
Vaginal oestrogen is preferred over continuous antibiotic prophylaxis
Low dose vaginal oestrogen needs no progestogen for endometrial protection
Imaging is reserved for haematuria, stones, residual volume or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Low dose vaginal oestrogen produces serum levels within the postmenopausal range, so it can be offered to most women with a history of oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer after discussion with their oncologist rather than being automatically withheld.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis does reduce episodes while it is taken, but benefit stops when it stops and it drives resistance in an organism that is currently fully sensitive. It is reserved for women in whom non antibiotic measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Treating each episode as it arises is what she is already doing, and it leaves the underlying mucosal change untouched so the pattern simply continues. Self start therapy is a reasonable adjunct but is not preventive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Increased fluid intake has modest supporting evidence and is worth advising, but cranberry products have not shown consistent benefit in trials and neither addresses the oestrogen deficient epithelium. These are adjuncts rather than the principal treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Oestrogen deficiency thins the urogenital epithelium and raises vaginal pH, which allows uropathogens to replace the protective lactobacilli, and topical replacement reverses both changes and significantly reduces recurrence. Systemic absorption from low dose vaginal preparations is minimal, so a progestogen is not required for endometrial protection. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Imaging and cystoscopy are indicated where there is haematuria between episodes, infection with urea splitting organisms, suspected stones or a significant post-void residual, none of which is present. Her tract has already been imaged and shown to be normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Contraceptive choice after birth is governed by two considerations that move on different timelines: venous thromboembolism risk, which is highest in the first three weeks and has largely resolved by six, and the effect of oestrogen on establishing lactation. Progestogen only pills, implants and injections do not affect milk supply and can be started at any time from immediately after birth, and both intrauterine device types can be inserted within the first 48 hours or from four weeks onwards. Combined hormonal methods are deferred to six weeks in a woman who is breastfeeding, and to three weeks in a woman who is not and has no additional thrombotic risk factors. Ovulation can return from about day 21 in a woman who is not fully breastfeeding, so a plan should be made before discharge even when the chosen method starts later.
key_points: Progestogen only methods can start immediately and do not affect milk supply
Combined methods are deferred to six weeks while breastfeeding
Combined methods may start at three weeks if not breastfeeding and low risk
Lactational amenorrhoea requires full breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and age under six months
Ovulation can precede the first postpartum period, so counsel before discharge
explanation.pearls: An intrauterine device inserted within 48 hours of birth is acceptable, but insertion between 48 hours and four weeks carries a markedly higher perforation and expulsion rate and should be avoided.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.rationale: Combined preparations are avoided in the first six weeks in a breastfeeding woman because oestrogen can reduce milk supply while lactation is being established, and the postpartum thrombotic risk remains elevated in the early weeks. A progestogen only method or an intrauterine device can be started now if she wants cover before then. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.rationale: Day 5 falls inside the period of greatest postpartum thrombotic risk and coincides with the establishment of milk supply, which oestrogen can suppress. The convenience of starting before discharge does not outweigh either concern. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.rationale: Three weeks is the usual earliest start for a woman who is not breastfeeding and has no additional thrombotic risk factors, and applying it here ignores the lactation consideration. The breastfeeding threshold is six weeks. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.rationale: Lactational amenorrhoea is only reliable while all three conditions hold together: full breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and an infant under six months. Presenting it as twelve months of cover misstates the method and invites exactly the unplanned pregnancy she is trying to avoid. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.rationale: Progestogen only methods do not affect milk supply and can be started immediately after birth, so withholding all hormonal options is unnecessarily restrictive. Only the oestrogen containing methods carry the lactation concern. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer presents with vague abdominal symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency and pelvic discomfort, and the persistence and newness of these symptoms in a woman over 50 is what should trigger investigation rather than their individual specificity. Initial assessment combines pelvic ultrasound with serum CA125, and these feed with menopausal status into the risk of malignancy index, where a score above 200 indicates referral to a gynaecological oncology centre. The reason the referral destination matters so much is that survival correlates with the completeness of cytoreduction achieved at the first operation, which is consistently better in specialist units. CA125 must be interpreted with care, since it rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and any peritoneal irritation, which is why the index weights it alongside imaging rather than using it alone.
key_points: Persistent new bloating and early satiety over 50 warrant investigation
Initial assessment is pelvic ultrasound plus serum CA125
The risk of malignancy index combines menopausal status, ultrasound and CA125
A score above 200 mandates referral to a gynaecological oncology unit
Survival depends on complete cytoreduction at the first operation
explanation.pearls: CA125 is raised in only about half of early stage ovarian cancers, so a normal value never excludes malignancy in a woman with a suspicious mass on ultrasound.

options.rationale: Cystectomy is an operation for a benign cyst in a woman wishing to preserve ovarian tissue, and performing it here risks rupturing a malignant cyst and upstaging the disease. Fertility preservation is not a consideration at this age. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

Interval surveillance is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst under 5 cm with a normal marker in a postmenopausal woman. With solid areas, ascites and a markedly raised marker, a three month delay allows progression of a disease whose outcome depends on early complete surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

Percutaneous sampling of an apparently operable ovarian mass risks seeding the peritoneum and the needle track, and the diagnosis is normally made at definitive surgery instead. Biopsy is reserved for advanced disease where chemotherapy will precede surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

Survival in ovarian cancer depends strongly on complete cytoreduction performed by a trained subspecialist, and operating outside such a unit is associated with incomplete staging and worse outcomes. The referral destination is itself part of the treatment decision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology and the CA125 value, and a score above 200 identifies a high probability of malignancy warranting referral to a specialist centre. Her postmenopausal status, multiple suspicious ultrasound features and markedly raised marker place her far above that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents early onset neonatal group B streptococcal sepsis and is most effective when the first dose is given at least four hours before birth. Benzylpenicillin is first choice, and the decision tree for a woman with a penicillin label turns entirely on how severe the reported reaction was. A low risk history is an isolated delayed rash without mucosal involvement, systemic features or blistering, and such women receive cefazolin, which shares no side chain with the penicillins and carries negligible cross reactivity. A high risk history, meaning anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory compromise or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, moves the choice to clindamycin if the isolate is proven susceptible and otherwise to vancomycin. Because most penicillin allergy labels are inaccurate, taking a proper allergy history in the antenatal period is a concrete clinical intervention rather than a formality.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line when no allergy label exists
Severity of the reported reaction determines the alternative chosen
Delayed rash without systemic features is a low risk history
Cefazolin shares no side chain with penicillins and is preferred in low risk allergy
Clindamycin requires demonstrated susceptibility of the isolate
explanation.pearls: Request clindamycin susceptibility at the time of the 36 week group B streptococcus swab for any woman with a penicillin allergy label, because the result is unavailable once she presents in labour.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is the agent of choice where no allergy exists, and a delayed rash is indeed low risk, but a recorded penicillin label is not simply overridden at the bedside in labour without formal assessment. The cephalosporin achieves comparable cover while respecting the label. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin is reserved for women at high risk of anaphylaxis whose isolate is resistant to clindamycin or whose susceptibility is unknown, and it crosses the placenta less reliably. Using it for a low risk rash history exposes mother and baby to a broader agent without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A delayed maculopapular rash without mucosal, respiratory or systemic involvement is a low risk history, and the cross reactivity between penicillins and cefazolin is negligible because they share no side chain, which her subsequent tolerance of cefalexin supports. Cefazolin crosses the placenta well and achieves adequate fetal levels, making it the preferred choice in low risk allergy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Clindamycin is an option only for severe allergy and only when the isolate has been shown susceptible, since resistance rates in group B streptococcus are appreciable and no susceptibility was requested here. Giving it blind risks ineffective prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Prophylaxis must be intravenous to achieve adequate and rapid amniotic fluid concentrations before birth, and the oral route cannot do this reliably. It also ignores the recorded allergy to the same drug class. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: A single course of antenatal betamethasone before preterm birth reduces respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death, and the effect is greatest when birth occurs between 24 hours and seven days after the course. The clinical difficulty arises with the substantial group of women who receive a course during a threatened preterm labour that then settles, and who represent again weeks later. Australian randomised evidence established that a single repeat course in that situation reduces respiratory morbidity, whereas weekly repetition reduces birthweight and head circumference without further respiratory gain. The decision therefore requires three conditions together: more than seven days since the previous course, a gestation still within the treatable range, and a genuine judgement that birth is likely within the next week. Corticosteroids also raise maternal blood glucose for several days, which matters when diabetes complicates the pregnancy.
key_points: Maximal benefit falls between 24 hours and seven days after administration
A single repeat course is supported when more than seven days have elapsed
Weekly repeated courses reduce birthweight and head circumference
The judgement that birth is likely within seven days is part of the indication
Maternal blood glucose rises for several days after a course
explanation.pearls: Australian practice was shaped by a randomised trial showing that one repeat betamethasone course reduced neonatal respiratory morbidity, which is why the repeat is offered once rather than on a weekly schedule.

options.rationale: Weekly repeated courses have been associated with reduced birthweight and smaller head circumference without additional respiratory benefit, so repetition is deliberately limited. The evidence supports a single repeat rather than a rolling schedule. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

The benefit of the original course wanes after about seven days, so a woman who did not give birth within that window and now faces imminent birth stands to gain from a repeat. Treating the first course as permanently sufficient forfeits that benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

The accepted gestational ceiling for a repeat course extends beyond 30 weeks, so this gestation does not exclude her. Respiratory morbidity remains substantial at this gestation and the treatment still reduces it. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

Membrane rupture is neither necessary nor sufficient as a trigger, since the decision rests on the likelihood of birth within the next seven days. Waiting for rupture may mean the course is given too late to take effect. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

A single repeat course is indicated when more than seven days have elapsed since the first, the woman remains below the gestational ceiling and birth is judged likely within the next seven days, all of which apply here. The Australian randomised evidence showed reduced respiratory distress and less oxygen requirement with a single repeat, without the growth effects seen with weekly dosing. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria with a midstream urine culture at the first antenatal visit is one of the few screening tests in pregnancy that clearly prevents a serious maternal complication. Progesterone mediated smooth muscle relaxation and mechanical compression by the gravid uterus produce ureteric dilatation and urinary stasis, so bacteria that would remain confined to the bladder outside pregnancy ascend readily to the kidneys. Untreated, a substantial minority of affected women develop pyelonephritis, which is associated with preterm birth, low birthweight, maternal sepsis and acute kidney injury. Antibiotic choice follows susceptibility while respecting pregnancy safety, and a test of cure culture is taken after treatment because persistent or recurrent bacteriuria is common and may require repeat treatment or suppressive prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy. Group B streptococcus isolated in the urine at any point is a separate matter and indicates intrapartum prophylaxis regardless of the swab result later in pregnancy.
key_points: Pregnancy is the main exception to not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria
Ureteric dilatation and stasis favour ascending infection
Untreated bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis in a substantial minority
A test of cure culture follows treatment because persistence is common
Group B streptococcus in urine mandates intrapartum prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Group B streptococcus cultured from the urine at any stage of pregnancy indicates heavy genital colonisation and is an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, irrespective of what the 36 week swab shows.

options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because up to a third of untreated women progress to pyelonephritis, with associated preterm birth and low birthweight, and treatment substantially reduces that risk. A test of cure culture after treatment confirms clearance, since persistence is common and warrants further courses or prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening, because the complication being prevented is ascending infection that often announces itself as established pyelonephritis. The screening program exists precisely to treat before symptoms occur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Leaving asymptomatic bacteriuria untreated is standard outside pregnancy, and in older adults and catheterised patients treating it causes harm without benefit. Pregnancy is the major exception because of the physiological ureteric dilatation and stasis that favour ascending infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A significant pure growth on a properly collected specimen is sufficient to act on, and requiring a second confirmatory culture delays treatment without improving accuracy. Repeat culture has a role as a test of cure rather than as a precondition for treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging is reserved for recurrent infection, suspected stones or structural abnormality, none of which is suggested by a single positive screening culture. It would delay a simple and effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage after 20 weeks is separated clinically by the presence or absence of pain and uterine tone: painless bright red bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus suggests placenta praevia, whereas pain with a tense tender uterus suggests abruption. A low lying placenta found at the morphology scan is common and most resolve as the lower segment develops, so the diagnosis is confirmed by transvaginal ultrasound in the third trimester, which is safe and more accurate than the transabdominal route. The governing rule of management is that no digital vaginal examination is performed until praevia has been excluded, since it can provoke catastrophic bleeding. A first bleed that settles in a stable woman is managed by admission, corticosteroids for lung maturity, anti-D for a woman who is rhesus negative, group and hold with attention to haemoglobin, and planned caesarean section, typically between 36 and 37 weeks or sooner if bleeding recurs.
key_points: Painless bleeding with a soft uterus suggests praevia; pain with a tense uterus suggests abruption
Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and confirms the placental position
No digital vaginal examination until praevia has been excluded
A settled first bleed is managed by admission with corticosteroids
Birth is by planned caesarean section, usually at 36 to 37 weeks
explanation.pearls: Ask about previous caesarean sections whenever praevia is diagnosed, because a placenta praevia overlying a uterine scar carries a substantially increased risk of placenta accreta spectrum and changes the planning of the birth entirely.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: Digital examination in the presence of a placenta covering the os can disrupt the placental edge and provoke torrential haemorrhage, and it is the single manoeuvre to avoid in this situation. Any assessment of the cervix is made by speculum or ultrasound instead. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: A first bleed that settles in a stable woman with a reassuring cardiotocograph is managed expectantly as an inpatient, because a further and heavier bleed can occur without warning and she needs to be where blood and theatre are available. Corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity since birth before term is now considerably more likely. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: Outpatient management is considered only after a period of inpatient stability in a woman who lives close to the hospital with ready transport and support. Discharging on the day of a first significant bleed leaves her distant from care when the next one occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: Immediate birth is reserved for maternal haemodynamic compromise, a non reassuring cardiotocograph or bleeding that does not settle, none of which applies. Delivering a stable 32 week pregnancy now would impose avoidable prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: A placenta covering the internal os is an absolute contraindication to labour and to vaginal birth, because the presenting part cannot descend without disrupting the placenta. Birth must be by caesarean section. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

explanation.summary: Most women with epilepsy have uncomplicated pregnancies, and the overriding principle is that uncontrolled convulsive seizures are more dangerous to mother and fetus than the anticonvulsants used to prevent them. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are the preferred agents because of comparatively reassuring malformation and neurodevelopmental data, while valproate is avoided wherever possible and topiramate carries cleft and growth restriction concerns. Lamotrigine is pharmacokinetically distinctive: oestrogen driven induction of glucuronidation increases its clearance so that plasma levels can fall by half or more as pregnancy advances, producing breakthrough seizures on a dose that was previously adequate. Levels are therefore checked before pregnancy where possible and through each trimester, with the dose increased to maintain the preconception concentration and reduced again over the first weeks after birth to avoid toxicity as clearance returns to baseline. High dose folic acid is started as soon as pregnancy is recognised, and women should be advised about safer bathing and infant handling practices.
key_points: Uncontrolled convulsive seizures pose greater risk than anticonvulsant exposure
Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are the preferred agents in pregnancy
Pregnancy raises lamotrigine clearance so levels fall substantially
Check levels each trimester and adjust the dose to the preconception level
Reduce the dose again in the weeks after birth as clearance normalises
explanation.pearls: Reduce the lamotrigine dose over the first two to three weeks postpartum towards the preconception dose, because clearance falls rapidly after birth and women who remain on the increased pregnancy dose develop toxicity with ataxia and diplopia.

options.rationale: Lamotrigine clearance rises markedly during pregnancy through induced glucuronidation, so levels fall progressively and seizures can recur on an unchanged dose, which makes scheduled level monitoring with dose adjustment the core of management. Continuing treatment is safer than stopping, because a generalised convulsion carries hypoxic risk to the fetus and a real risk of maternal death. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Lamotrigine is among the anticonvulsants with the most reassuring data on major congenital malformation, and abrupt cessation in a woman with a history of bilateral tonic clonic seizures risks status epilepticus. Stopping poses a far greater threat to both than continuing. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Valproate carries the highest rates of major congenital malformation and of impaired neurodevelopment of any anticonvulsant and is specifically avoided in pregnancy wherever an alternative exists. Switching towards it would be the worst available choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Halving the dose moves in exactly the wrong direction given that pregnancy already lowers levels substantially, and it would leave her subtherapeutic at the point her seizure risk is rising. Partial dosing delivers the risks of exposure without the protection. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Continuing is right but doing so blindly ignores the pharmacokinetic change that distinguishes this drug, and breakthrough seizures in the second and third trimesters are the predictable result. Lamotrigine is one of the anticonvulsants where level monitoring genuinely alters management. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Graves disease in pregnancy requires balancing the harms of uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis against the harms of the drugs that control it, and the balance shifts with gestation. Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with an embryopathy comprising aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia and dysmorphic features, with risk concentrated during organogenesis, so propylthiouracil is preferred through the first trimester. Propylthiouracil in turn carries a rare but serious risk of fulminant hepatic failure, which is why many units switch back after the first trimester. Both drugs cross the placenta, so the aim is the lowest dose that keeps free thyroxine in the upper part of the normal range, accepting a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone, and block and replace regimens are avoided because the higher antithyroid dose reaches the fetus while the replacement thyroxine does not. Thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies should be measured because they cross the placenta and can cause fetal or neonatal thyrotoxicosis even in a mother who has been rendered euthyroid by surgery or radioiodine.
key_points: Carbimazole embryopathy risk is concentrated during first trimester organogenesis
Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester despite hepatotoxicity risk
Aim for free thyroxine in the upper normal range on the lowest effective dose
Block and replace regimens cause fetal hypothyroidism and are avoided
Receptor antibodies cross the placenta and can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies even in a woman previously treated with radioiodine or surgery, because the antibodies persist and cross the placenta to cause fetal thyrotoxicosis in a mother who is herself euthyroid or hypothyroid.

options.rationale: Stopping altogether risks relapse of thyrotoxicosis, which is associated with miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction and maternal heart failure. Withdrawal is considered only in women with mild disease in long remission and is not a default on discovering pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Carbimazole and its active metabolite are associated with a specific embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia, with the risk concentrated in the period of organogenesis, so propylthiouracil is preferred through the first trimester. Because propylthiouracil carries a small risk of severe hepatotoxicity, most units switch back afterwards, which is why the plan is framed as a change with later review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

This leaves her on the agent associated with embryopathy during precisely the weeks when organogenesis occurs. Carbimazole becomes the preferred drug again after the first trimester, not during it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A block and replace regimen requires higher antithyroid drug doses, and since these cross the placenta while thyroxine does so poorly, the fetus is rendered hypothyroid with goitre. It is specifically avoided in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Surgery is reserved for severe or refractory disease or drug intolerance and, when needed, is timed to the second trimester to minimise miscarriage and preterm labour risk. It is disproportionate for well controlled disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Fibroids grow under oestrogen stimulation during pregnancy, and a large fibroid can outgrow its blood supply and undergo haemorrhagic infarction, known as red or carneous degeneration. The presentation is severe pain localised precisely over the fibroid, often with a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and raised inflammatory markers, which makes infection the obvious but incorrect first thought. The features that separate it are tenderness confined to the fibroid with a soft non-tender uterus elsewhere, intact membranes, a closed cervix and a reassuring cardiotocograph. Treatment is supportive with adequate analgesia, hydration and observation, and the pain settles over one to two weeks, with nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs limited in duration and avoided after 32 weeks because of premature ductal constriction. Surgery is avoided because the gravid uterus bleeds heavily, and fibroids are reassessed after the puerperium when they commonly shrink.
key_points: Fibroids enlarge under oestrogen stimulation and can outgrow their blood supply
Pain is sharply localised over the fibroid with a soft uterus elsewhere
Low grade fever and raised inflammatory markers mimic infection
Management is analgesia, hydration and observation over one to two weeks
Myomectomy in pregnancy risks torrential haemorrhage and is avoided
explanation.pearls: Avoid nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs after 32 weeks and limit courses to about 48 hours before then, because prolonged exposure constricts the ductus arteriosus and reduces fetal urine output causing oligohydramnios.

options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a high risk of torrential haemorrhage from the vascular gravid uterus and of pregnancy loss, so it is avoided except in extreme circumstances such as a torted pedunculated fibroid. The pain here is self-limiting and does not justify that risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

Chorioamnionitis produces generalised uterine tenderness with maternal and fetal tachycardia and usually follows membrane rupture, whereas her tenderness is confined to the fibroid with intact membranes and a closed cervix. The mild fever and inflammatory response here reflect tissue infarction rather than infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

Red degeneration occurs when a fibroid outgrows its blood supply during the rapid growth of the second trimester, producing localised pain with a low grade fever and mildly raised inflammatory markers that mimic infection. It is self-limiting over one to two weeks, so management is adequate analgesia, hydration and observation, avoiding prolonged nonsteroidal use beyond 32 weeks because of ductal constriction. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

Embolisation is contraindicated in pregnancy because it would compromise the uteroplacental circulation and expose the fetus to radiation. It is a treatment for symptomatic fibroids outside pregnancy in women who have completed childbearing. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

Birth at 22 weeks would be pre viable and the underlying process is a self-limiting one that resolves with time and analgesia. There is no maternal or fetal compromise that would justify ending the pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Preconception care for a woman with epilepsy balances two risks that pull in opposite directions: the teratogenicity of antiepileptic drugs and the harm caused by uncontrolled seizures. For most women established on an agent with a favourable profile, continuing treatment is safer than stopping it, and any change to the regimen is planned with a neurologist before conception rather than reactively in early pregnancy. High dose folic acid at 5 mg daily is recommended for women on antiepileptic therapy, in contrast to the 0.5 mg standard dose, and should begin at least one month before conception. Neural tube closure completes before most pregnancies are recognised, which is why the timing matters.
key_points: Seizure control is protective for the pregnancy; abrupt self cessation is the greater immediate danger
Folic acid 5 mg daily rather than 0.5 mg for women on antiepileptic drugs, previous affected pregnancy, diabetes or a body mass index above 30 kg/m2
Sodium valproate is avoided in anyone of reproductive potential because of malformation and neurodevelopmental risk
Lamotrigine concentrations fall substantially during pregnancy and require monitoring with dose adjustment
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises through pregnancy so levels can fall by more than half by the third trimester; establish a preconception baseline concentration while she is seizure free, because that is the target to titrate against later.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after three years of control risks status epilepticus and loss of her driving licence, and a generalised seizure in pregnancy causes fetal hypoxia and placental abruption. Withdrawal is a specialist decision made before conception is attempted, not a self directed one. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

Valproate carries the highest risk of major congenital malformation and neurodevelopmental harm of the commonly used antiepileptics and should be avoided in anyone who could become pregnant. Moving towards it is the opposite of the required direction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Restarting the drug is right but 0.5 mg is the dose for women at standard risk. Antiepileptic therapy places her in the higher risk group for whom 5 mg daily is recommended, and the folate antagonism of several agents is the reason. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

Uncontrolled seizures carry a greater risk to mother and fetus than lamotrigine, which is among the antiepileptics with the lowest teratogenic risk, so the drug is resumed rather than stopped. Women taking any antiepileptic are advised to take the higher 5 mg folic acid dose from at least one month before conception through the first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

Neural tube closure is complete by 28 days after conception, which is usually before a woman knows she is pregnant, so folate supplementation and drug optimisation must be in place beforehand. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

explanation.summary: Pertussis causes its greatest mortality in infants under 6 months, who are too young to have completed their own primary course, so protection in those first weeks depends on maternal antibody acquired across the placenta. A pertussis containing vaccine is therefore recommended in every pregnancy, irrespective of when the woman was last vaccinated, because antibody levels fall substantially within a year. The recommended window is 20 to 32 weeks, which allows time for the maternal antibody response and its transfer before birth while still covering preterm delivery. Vaccinating household contacts is complementary but does not replace maternal vaccination.
key_points: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy, not once per lifetime
The window of 20 to 32 weeks balances antibody production against the risk of preterm birth
Maternal vaccination is more effective at protecting the newborn than vaccinating contacts
It is safe during breastfeeding and can be given postpartum if missed in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: If a woman presents after 32 weeks, still vaccinate rather than defer to the postnatal period: a late dose transfers less antibody than an ideally timed one but still transfers some, and the alternative leaves the infant with none at all.

options.rationale: Antibody from a dose given three years ago has waned and is not transferred in protective quantity to the current fetus, which is why a dose is recommended in each pregnancy rather than once only. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Postpartum vaccination protects the mother from becoming a source of infection but gives the newborn no transplacental antibody, leaving the infant unprotected during the first weeks when the disease is most lethal. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

A dose this late leaves insufficient time for maternal antibody production and placental transfer before birth, particularly if she delivers early, which is why the recommended window closes at 32 weeks. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Vaccinating close contacts reduces exposure and is recommended alongside maternal vaccination, but it does not provide the infant with circulating antibody and is markedly less effective on its own. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

A pertussis containing vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of previous doses, because the protection that matters is the transfer of maternal antibody to this particular fetus, and antibody levels wane within months. The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, which maximises transplacental transfer before birth. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity, not zygosity, determines the risk profile and the surveillance plan of a twin pregnancy, because monochorionic twins share a placenta with vascular anastomoses and are at risk of twin to twin transfusion, selective growth restriction and anaemia polycythaemia sequence. It is determined by ultrasound between 11 and 13 weeks, when the membrane insertion shows either a thick triangular wedge of placental tissue indicating two chorions or a thin T shaped junction indicating one. After about 14 weeks the sign becomes progressively harder to identify. Monochorionic pregnancies require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks and earlier planned birth, whereas dichorionic pregnancies are scanned less frequently.
key_points: Chorionicity drives management; zygosity is largely of academic interest
The membrane sign is most reliable between 11 and 13 weeks
Monochorionic pregnancies need fortnightly surveillance from 16 weeks
Two sacs on an early scan does not exclude a shared placenta
explanation.pearls: Make sure chorionicity is recorded in the handheld record and on every subsequent report: when the information is lost, later scans default to treating the pregnancy as monochorionic, and a woman can end up with months of unnecessary fortnightly surveillance or, far worse, a missed diagnosis of twin to twin transfusion.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Chorionicity determines the entire antenatal plan and is most reliably established between 11 and 13 weeks, when the membrane insertion can be seen as either a thick triangular projection of placental tissue or a thin T shaped junction. Determination becomes progressively less reliable as gestation advances, so the window should not be missed. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Cell free DNA testing screens for common aneuploidies and does not establish chorionicity, which is an anatomical question about the placenta rather than a genetic one. Zygosity and chorionicity are also not the same thing. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Waiting until the morphology scan misses the window in which the membrane is most easily characterised and delays the fortnightly surveillance that a monochorionic pregnancy requires from 16 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Two sacs seen early may still represent a monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy, and identical twins are commonly diamniotic, so sac number alone does not establish either zygosity or chorionicity. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Intensive surveillance is appropriate for a monochorionic pregnancy but represents considerable unnecessary scanning and anxiety if the pregnancy proves dichorionic, so the chorionicity is established first. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Rubella serology is checked at booking in every Australian pregnancy because congenital rubella syndrome is devastating and entirely preventable. A live rubella containing vaccine cannot be given during pregnancy, so a non immune woman is vaccinated immediately after birth, before discharge, while she is still in contact with the service. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication. She should be advised to avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards, although inadvertent vaccination in early pregnancy has not been shown to cause congenital rubella syndrome and is not an indication for termination.
key_points: Vaccinate postpartum before discharge, because the opportunity is easily lost at follow up
Live rubella containing vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but safe during breastfeeding
Advise avoiding pregnancy for 28 days after the dose
Immunoglobulin is not a substitute for vaccination and has no role without an exposure
explanation.pearls: A second dose is needed for durable protection in someone with no documented childhood immunisation, so arrange the second measles mumps rubella dose at least 28 days later rather than assuming the postnatal dose has completed the course.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin provides short lived passive protection after an exposure and does not generate the lasting immunity needed to protect a subsequent pregnancy. It has no role in a woman who has not been exposed. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Rubella containing vaccine is a live vaccine that cannot be given during pregnancy, so the immediate postpartum period before discharge is the standard opportunity to protect future pregnancies, and it is safe during breastfeeding. She is advised to avoid pregnancy for 28 days after the dose. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to live rubella containing vaccine, and deferring until weaning risks a further pregnancy occurring while she is still susceptible. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Repeating the antibody test will not change a non immune result obtained in pregnancy and postpones the vaccination past the point at which she is most reliably in contact with the health service. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Household immunity limits exposure but does not protect the fetus of a susceptible mother, and the infant is not eligible for a rubella containing vaccine until 12 months of age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by first establishing whether secondary sexual characteristics are present and then measuring gonadotrophins, which separates ovarian from central causes. A high follicle stimulating hormone with absent breast development indicates primary ovarian failure, and when it occurs alongside short stature and characteristic features such as a webbed neck, wide carrying angle and widely spaced nipples the diagnosis is a sex chromosome abnormality. Karyotype is therefore the definitive investigation. It matters practically because the presence of Y chromosome material mandates gonadectomy for malignancy risk, and because associated cardiac, renal, thyroid and hearing problems need screening.
key_points: High gonadotrophins localise the lesion to the gonad; low gonadotrophins point to the hypothalamus or pituitary
Short stature with primary amenorrhoea should prompt karyotype rather than further hormonal testing
Y chromosome material in a phenotypic female requires gonadectomy because of gonadoblastoma risk
Associated anomalies include bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, autoimmune thyroid disease and conductive hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography at diagnosis even when femoral pulses are normal and blood pressures are equal: bicuspid aortic valve occurs in up to a third of these girls and predisposes to aortic dissection in later pregnancy.

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary is indicated when gonadotrophins are low, indicating a central cause. Here they are high, which localises the problem to the ovary and makes a pituitary lesion very unlikely. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

Androgen measurement is directed at virilisation or at a disorder of androgen action, and she has neither hirsutism nor clitoromegaly. It would not explain the short stature or the raised gonadotrophins. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

A raised follicle stimulating hormone with absent secondary sexual characteristics identifies primary gonadal failure, and in a girl with short stature and the associated dysmorphic features the cause is a sex chromosome abnormality until proven otherwise. The karyotype also determines whether Y chromosome material is present, which carries a risk of gonadal malignancy and changes management. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

A withdrawal bleed test assesses whether the endometrium has been oestrogenised, but the oestradiol is already known to be undetectable so the result is predictable and adds nothing. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

Coeliac disease is a recognised cause of short stature and delayed puberty, but it acts through chronic illness and undernutrition and produces low rather than high gonadotrophins, and her body mass index is normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

explanation.summary: Invasive group A streptococcal infection remains a leading cause of direct maternal death in Australia and characteristically presents with an extremely rapid course in the first few days after birth. The clues are severe pain out of proportion to findings, high fever with rigors, uterine tenderness with offensive lochia, and a household contact with pharyngitis, often in a young child. A low rather than high white cell count is a recognised and ominous feature. Management is immediate resuscitation with benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin, the latter for its suppression of exotoxin synthesis, alongside cultures, senior involvement and consideration of source control.
key_points: A falling or low white cell count in sepsis is a marker of severity, not of mild disease
Clindamycin is added for exotoxin suppression, not for its spectrum
A household contact with sore throat is a classic and frequently missed piece of history
Consider intravenous immunoglobulin and early surgical review if toxic shock or necrotising infection develops
explanation.pearls: Ask every septic postnatal woman about sore throat in the household: group A streptococcus is carried in the throats of young children, and that single question often separates this diagnosis from ordinary polymicrobial endometritis before any culture returns.

options.rationale: This combination is reasonable empirical cover for polymicrobial endometritis but lacks the antitoxin effect of a protein synthesis inhibitor, which is what limits toxic shock in invasive streptococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral therapy is inadequate in a woman with hypotension, a raised lactate and organ dysfunction, in whom gastrointestinal absorption is unreliable and delay costs survival. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cultures must be taken but mortality in invasive streptococcal sepsis rises with every hour of delay to effective therapy, and results take at least 12 to 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fulminant sepsis within 48 hours of birth with uterine tenderness, offensive lochia, a low white cell count and a recent household sore throat points to invasive group A streptococcal infection, for which benzylpenicillin is the definitive agent and clindamycin is added to suppress exotoxin production. Treatment is given immediately after cultures rather than after imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

An aminoglycoside gives no useful cover against group A streptococcus, and imaging to look for retained products should follow resuscitation and antibiotics rather than precede them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Counselling after obstetric anal sphincter injury turns on whether the woman is symptomatic and what objective testing shows. A woman who is fully continent with a normal endoanal ultrasound and normal manometry can be offered vaginal birth with a small risk of recurrence. A woman with persisting incontinence, a demonstrable sphincter defect or reduced squeeze pressure should be offered planned caesarean, because a further vaginal birth carries a substantial risk of permanent worsening. Secondary sphincter repair is reserved for women with severe symptoms who have completed childbearing, since its benefit degrades over time and is lost with another vaginal birth.
key_points: Symptoms plus objective sphincter deficiency is the combination that shifts the recommendation to caesarean
Asymptomatic women with normal investigations may be offered vaginal birth
Elective episiotomy does not reliably protect a previously injured sphincter
Flatus incontinence counts as a symptom and should be asked about directly
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about flatus control and faecal urgency rather than asking whether she is incontinent: women very rarely volunteer these symptoms, and urgency with a plateaued physiotherapy response is what converts a routine counselling conversation into a recommendation for caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not reliably protect a previously injured sphincter, and subjecting an already symptomatic and structurally deficient sphincter to another vaginal birth is the situation in which continence most often deteriorates permanently. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Pelvic floor physiotherapy is valuable and should continue, but she has already had a course with a plateau in response, and conservative therapy cannot restore a structural sphincter defect before another vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Avoiding forceps reduces but does not remove the risk to the sphincter, since spontaneous birth also stretches and can further disrupt a deficient muscle, and the plan gives no protection if instrumental birth becomes necessary. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Delayed sphincter repair is considered for severe incontinence in women who have completed their families, because its results deteriorate over time and are undone by subsequent vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: A woman who remains symptomatic after a previous obstetric anal sphincter injury, with objective evidence of a persisting defect and reduced squeeze pressure, should be offered planned caesarean because a further vaginal birth risks irreversible deterioration to frank faecal incontinence. Women who are asymptomatic with normal investigations can be offered vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)

explanation.summary: Fertility falls sharply but does not disappear in the late forties and early fifties, and unintended pregnancy at this age carries high maternal and fetal risk. The simplest and safest rule is to continue contraception until age 55, at which point it can be stopped regardless of bleeding pattern and without hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea while taking a progestogen only method is caused by the method and says nothing about ovarian activity. Combined hormonal contraception is generally discontinued at age 50 in favour of progestogen only or intrauterine methods.
key_points: Age 55 is the point at which contraception can be stopped without testing
Amenorrhoea on progestogen is method induced and is not evidence of menopause
Follicle stimulating hormone testing is optional from age 50 on progestogen only methods but is unreliable in isolation
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system fitted at 45 or older may be retained until 55 if used for contraception alone
explanation.pearls: If she later needs hormone replacement therapy for vasomotor symptoms, remember that standard hormone replacement is not contraceptive: she needs a separate contraceptive method alongside it until 55.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause
Australasian Menopause Society: Contraception and the perimenopause

options.rationale: Contraception is recommended until age 55, by which age natural conception is exceptionally rare, and it can then be stopped without any hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea on a progestogen only pill is caused by the pill itself and cannot be used as evidence that ovulation has ceased. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.rationale: Amenorrhoea is an expected effect of continuous progestogen and does not indicate loss of ovarian function, so stopping on that basis leaves her at risk of a late and unintended pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.rationale: Measuring follicle stimulating hormone is an option in women aged 50 or over using progestogen only methods, but results fluctuate widely in the perimenopause and a raised value does not exclude a subsequent ovulation. Continuing to 55 avoids the ambiguity altogether. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided from age 50 because the cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks outweigh its benefits, and she has no indication for oestrogen. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.rationale: Barrier methods are far less effective than a progestogen only pill she is already taking without problems, and there is no clinical reason to downgrade her contraceptive efficacy at this stage. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

explanation.summary: Vasomotor symptoms after breast cancer treatment are often more severe than those of natural menopause, because ovarian function is abruptly lost through chemotherapy and endocrine therapy adds its own effect. Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after hormone receptor positive disease, so management relies on non hormonal options, of which the serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors and gabapentin have the best evidence. Some selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, particularly paroxetine and fluoxetine, are potent inhibitors of cytochrome P450 2D6 and reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite. Venlafaxine and desvenlafaxine have minimal effect on that enzyme and are therefore preferred in women taking tamoxifen.
key_points: Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer
Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit cytochrome P450 2D6 and can undermine tamoxifen
Venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine and gabapentin are the preferred non hormonal options
Cognitive behavioural therapy has evidence for reducing the impact of flushes
explanation.pearls: Vaginal oestrogen is a separate question from systemic therapy: low dose vaginal preparations for genitourinary symptoms are often acceptable after discussion with the treating oncologist, even in women for whom systemic oestrogen is firmly contraindicated.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer because of the risk of stimulating recurrence, regardless of how severe the vasomotor symptoms are. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.rationale: Venlafaxine has the best evidence among non hormonal agents for reducing vasomotor symptom frequency and severity and is a preferred choice in women taking tamoxifen because it does not meaningfully inhibit the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite. Her symptom burden is well past the point at which lifestyle measures alone suffice. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.rationale: Paroxetine does reduce flushes but is a potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 2D6, which converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, so it risks reducing the effectiveness of her cancer treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.rationale: Evidence of benefit is weak and inconsistent, and preparations with oestrogenic activity are generally avoided after hormone receptor positive breast cancer. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.rationale: Lifestyle measures have already been tried without benefit and are insufficient for a symptom burden that is disrupting sleep nightly and causing her to withdraw from work and social life. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism occurring in pregnancy is treated with therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for at least three months in total and for a minimum of six weeks after birth, whichever period is longer. The postpartum rule exists because thrombotic risk peaks in the puerperium rather than falling at delivery. Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding and can be used postnatally, but direct oral anticoagulants are avoided because they are excreted in breast milk with limited safety data. Pregnancy counts as a transient provoking factor, so indefinite anticoagulation is not required, but prophylaxis is recommended in subsequent pregnancies and the puerperium.
key_points: At least three months total and at least six weeks postpartum, whichever is longer
Risk of thrombosis is highest in the first six weeks after birth, not during pregnancy
Low molecular weight heparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding; direct oral anticoagulants are not
A pregnancy associated event indicates thromboprophylaxis in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: Plan the peripartum interruption explicitly: therapeutic low molecular weight heparin is usually withheld for 24 hours before planned birth or neuraxial block, and a woman on treatment dose should have a documented plan converting her to a shorter acting strategy as induction approaches.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: The six weeks after birth are the period of greatest risk because of venous stasis, vessel injury and the procoagulant state, so stopping at delivery removes protection precisely when it is most needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended during breastfeeding because of limited safety data and measurable excretion into milk, so they are avoided in a woman who intends to breastfeed. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Pregnancy associated venous thromboembolism is treated for a minimum of three months in total and for at least six weeks after birth, whichever is longer, because the postpartum period carries the highest thrombotic risk of the whole pregnancy. She was diagnosed at 30 weeks, so six weeks postpartum takes her past the three month minimum. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Dose reduction applies to women receiving prophylaxis for risk factors, not to treatment of an established event within the same pregnancy, which requires therapeutic intensity for the full course. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Lifelong treatment is reserved for unprovoked recurrent events or high risk thrombophilia. Pregnancy is a transient major provoking factor, so a defined course is appropriate with prophylaxis considered in future pregnancies. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
